card.summary: The plant that put holes in a million living rooms. A monstera deliciosa is a climbing aroid from the rainforests of southern Mexico and Central America, where it hauls itself up tree trunks and grows leaves the size of a bin lid.
card.light: Bright indirect light, which in practice means a metre or two back from an east or west window, or right up against a north one. Monsteras will survive in low light and simply stop earning their name: the new leaves come out smaller and solid, with no splits. Direct midday sun bleaches them to a pale khaki.
card.water: Water when the top 5 cm of mix is dry, then water until it runs out of the bottom. Monsteras would rather be a day late than a day early. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Happy at normal room humidity; better above 50%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C) and out of cold drafts.
card.soil: Monsteras are climbers that root into bark in the wild, not into soil. A peat-only compost holds water against the roots and is the usual reason a healthy plant turns yellow. Cut potting soil half-and-half with orchid bark and perlite, or buy a ready-made aroid mix.
card.feeding: A balanced liquid feed at half strength, every second or third watering in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Repot when roots come out of the drainage holes, in spring. Go up one pot size only — a monstera in too big a pot sits wet. Give it a moss pole at the same time: aerial roots that find something to climb produce noticeably larger, better-fenestrated leaves.

common_problems.problem: Yellow leaves, usually the oldest ones first
common_problems.fix: Overwatering, or a mix that holds water. The roots have been wet long enough to start dying back. Let it dry out further between waterings, and repot into something chunkier if the mix stays soggy for days.

common_problems.problem: New leaves come out small and with no splits
common_problems.fix: Not enough light, or nothing to climb. Move it closer to the window and give it a moss pole. Fenestration is a maturity signal; the plant withholds it when conditions say stay small.

common_problems.problem: Brown crispy edges
common_problems.fix: Dry air, or a build-up of salts from tap water and fertiliser. Raise humidity, and flush the pot thoroughly with plain water every few months.

common_problems.problem: Fine webbing between stems, leaves stippled pale
common_problems.fix: Spider mites, which arrive in dry warm air. Shower the whole plant, then treat every five days for three weeks — one treatment never gets the eggs.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and people if chewed — the sap carries insoluble calcium oxalate crystals, which burn the mouth and throat. Keep it off the floor if anything in the house tastes its way through life.

card.summary: The heartleaf philodendron: a trailing vine with soft heart-shaped leaves that has been sold as a houseplant for over a century, largely because it is very hard to kill. It grows in less light than almost anything else here and roots from any cutting.
card.light: Bright indirect light suits them, and most philodendrons cope with genuinely dim corners better than a monstera will — they just grow slower and stretch. Variegated forms are the exception: white and pink tissue cannot photosynthesise, so those plants need more light than their green siblings, not less.
card.water: Water when the top third of the pot is dry. Philodendrons wilt visibly when genuinely thirsty and recover within hours, which makes them easy to read. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Fine at room humidity, faster growth above 60%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C) and out of cold drafts.
card.soil: Almost all of them climb or creep rather than sit in deep soil, so the roots want air. Half potting compost, half bark and perlite is the standard recipe. Crawlers like gloriosum want a shallow wide pot rather than a deep one — the rhizome runs along the surface.
card.feeding: Balanced liquid feed at half strength every third watering through the growing season.
card.repotting: Every spring or two, one size up. A philodendron that has filled its pot pushes roots out of the drainage holes and dries out within a day or two of watering — that is the signal.

common_problems.problem: Long bare stems with leaves far apart
common_problems.fix: Too little light. The plant is reaching. Move it brighter and cut the leggy growth back — it will branch from the nodes below the cut.

common_problems.problem: Yellow lower leaves
common_problems.fix: Usually overwatering; occasionally just age, one leaf at a time. If several go at once, check the roots. Brown and soft means rot; trim them and repot into fresh airy mix.

common_problems.problem: Variegation fading back to plain green
common_problems.fix: Not enough light for the plant to afford the white tissue. Give it more light, and prune back to a node that still shows variegation — the plant grows on from the last variegated point.

common_problems.problem: Brown tips on new leaves that were fine in the old pot
common_problems.fix: Low humidity while the leaf was still unfurling. Group plants together or run a humidifier while new leaves open; the damage is cosmetic and permanent on that leaf.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and people if chewed — the sap carries insoluble calcium oxalate crystals, which burn the mouth and throat. Keep it off the floor if anything in the house tastes its way through life.

common_problems.problem: Long bare stems with leaves far apart
common_problems.fix: Too little light. The plant is reaching. Move it brighter and cut the leggy growth back — it will branch from the nodes below the cut.

common_problems.problem: Yellow lower leaves
common_problems.fix: Usually overwatering; occasionally just age, one leaf at a time. If several go at once, check the roots. Brown and soft means rot; trim them and repot into fresh airy mix.

common_problems.problem: Brown tips on new leaves that were fine in the old pot
common_problems.fix: Low humidity while the leaf was still unfurling. Group plants together or run a humidifier while new leaves open; the damage is cosmetic and permanent on that leaf.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and people if chewed — the sap carries insoluble calcium oxalate crystals, which burn the mouth and throat. Keep it off the floor if anything in the house tastes its way through life.

card.water: Water when the top third of the pot is dry. Philodendrons wilt visibly when genuinely thirsty and recover within hours, which makes them easy to read. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Fine at room humidity, faster growth above 60%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C) and out of cold drafts.
card.soil: Almost all of them climb or creep rather than sit in deep soil, so the roots want air. Half potting compost, half bark and perlite is the standard recipe. Crawlers like gloriosum want a shallow wide pot rather than a deep one — the rhizome runs along the surface.
card.feeding: Balanced liquid feed at half strength every third watering through the growing season.
card.repotting: Every spring or two, one size up. A philodendron that has filled its pot pushes roots out of the drainage holes and dries out within a day or two of watering — that is the signal.

common_problems.problem: Long bare stems with leaves far apart
common_problems.fix: Too little light. The plant is reaching. Move it brighter and cut the leggy growth back — it will branch from the nodes below the cut.

common_problems.problem: Yellow lower leaves
common_problems.fix: Usually overwatering; occasionally just age, one leaf at a time. If several go at once, check the roots. Brown and soft means rot; trim them and repot into fresh airy mix.

common_problems.problem: Variegation fading back to plain green
common_problems.fix: Not enough light for the plant to afford the white tissue. Give it more light, and prune back to a node that still shows variegation — the plant grows on from the last variegated point.

common_problems.problem: Brown tips on new leaves that were fine in the old pot
common_problems.fix: Low humidity while the leaf was still unfurling. Group plants together or run a humidifier while new leaves open; the damage is cosmetic and permanent on that leaf.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and people if chewed — the sap carries insoluble calcium oxalate crystals, which burn the mouth and throat. Keep it off the floor if anything in the house tastes its way through life.

card.summary: Still sold as Philodendron selloum, and still called a tree philodendron, though botanists moved it to Thaumatophyllum in 2018. It is a self-heading plant rather than a vine: a thick woody trunk with a crown of deeply cut leaves, spreading wider than it is tall.
card.light: Brighter than most philodendrons: this is a self-heading plant from open forest edges, and it will take morning sun happily. In dim light the leaf stalks stretch out until the plant flops.

card.summary: Pothos, golden pothos, devil's ivy — the plant given to people who say they kill everything. It trails, it climbs, it roots in a glass of water, and it puts up with light levels that would finish most houseplants.
card.light: Pothos is the plant that made 'tolerates low light' a cliché, and it earns it — but tolerating is not thriving. In a dark spot the leaves come smaller and the variegation fades; in bright indirect light the vines run and the pattern is crisp.
card.water: Water when the top half of the pot is dry — pothos droops its whole canopy when thirsty and stands back up within a couple of hours of a drink. As a starting point, water every 8 days.
card.humidity: Indifferent. Ordinary room air is fine.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C) and away from cold windows in winter.
card.soil: Pothos is not fussy. Ordinary compost with perlite mixed through for drainage does the job; it will also grow indefinitely in a jar of water, though a plant raised in water sulks if you later pot it into soil.
card.feeding: A balanced feed at half strength once a month in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every other spring. If the vines have gone long and bare at the top, cut them back hard at repotting time and push the cuttings into the same pot — that is how a full, bushy pothos is made.

common_problems.problem: Yellow leaves scattered through the plant
common_problems.fix: Overwatering. Pothos is much more often killed by kindness than by neglect. Let it dry out properly between waterings and make sure the pot actually drains.

common_problems.problem: Variegation disappearing, new leaves plain green
common_problems.fix: Not enough light. Move it brighter. Cut back to the last well-marked leaf; all-green growth will otherwise take over, because it grows faster.

common_problems.problem: Long stretches of bare vine
common_problems.fix: Light coming from one direction and no pruning. Cut the bare vines back to 15 cm; new shoots come from the nodes below the cut.

common_problems.problem: Black soft patches at the base of the stems
common_problems.fix: Root rot from standing water. Take healthy cuttings from the top of the vines, root those, and start again — a rotted crown rarely recovers.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and people if chewed — the sap carries insoluble calcium oxalate crystals, which burn the mouth and throat. Keep it off the floor if anything in the house tastes its way through life.

card.summary: A close relative of pothos that splits its leaves as it matures, so an established plant looks like a slender monstera. The blue-leaved form, 'Cebu Blue', is the one most people buy — juvenile leaves have a metallic blue sheen that it loses as it climbs and splits.

card.summary: The flamingo flower, the anthurium sold in supermarkets everywhere. What looks like a waxy red flower is a spathe — a modified leaf — around the true flowers on the spadix, and each one lasts for weeks.
card.light: Bright indirect light. The flowering kinds need it to keep producing spathes; the velvet-leaved ones scorch easily and want the same brightness filtered through a sheer curtain.
card.water: Water when the top of the mix is dry to the touch, and let it drain completely. In a bark mix that is often twice a week; in soil it would be a death sentence. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: 60% and up. This is the genus where humidity actually decides the outcome.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C); keep it above 60°F (15°C) and away from drafts and heaters.
card.soil: Anthuriums are epiphytes. The mix should look wrong: mostly orchid bark and perlite with a little coir, loose enough that water pours straight through. Standard compost suffocates them within a season.
card.feeding: A weak orchid feed every second watering while growing.
card.repotting: Every year or two, into a pot barely larger than the root ball. Bury the stem slightly deeper each time — anthuriums creep upward and go bald at the base otherwise.

common_problems.problem: Brown crispy leaf edges
common_problems.fix: Air too dry, or tap water minerals building up. Raise humidity above 60% and water with rain or filtered water if your tap is hard.

common_problems.problem: No flowers for months
common_problems.fix: Not enough light, or not enough phosphorus. Move it brighter and switch to a feed with a higher middle number through spring and summer.

common_problems.problem: Yellowing leaves with a soft brown base
common_problems.fix: Rot, almost always from a mix that holds water. Repot into bark and perlite, cutting away any root that is brown and mushy.

common_problems.problem: A bald woody stem with leaves only at the top
common_problems.fix: Normal upward creep. Repot deeper, or cut the top off below a set of aerial roots and re-root it.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and people if chewed — the sap carries insoluble calcium oxalate crystals, which burn the mouth and throat. Keep it off the floor if anything in the house tastes its way through life.

card.light: Bright indirect light — more than people give them. An alocasia in a dim room loses a leaf for every new one it makes and slowly winds down to nothing. Direct afternoon sun, though, burns holes in those thin leaves.
card.water: Water when the top third dries, and never leave the pot standing in a saucer of water. Alocasias also drip water from their leaf tips in the morning — that is guttation, and it means the roots are working, not that anything is wrong. As a starting point, water every 6 days.
card.humidity: 60% and above, or spider mites will find it.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C); keep it above 60°F (15°C). A cold spell often makes it drop leaves and go dormant.
card.soil: Alocasias grow from a corm, and a corm sitting in wet compost rots. Use a very open mix and a pot with real drainage. Many growers keep them in semi-hydroponics for exactly this reason.
card.feeding: Balanced feed at half strength every second or third watering, spring through summer only.
card.repotting: Once a year in spring. Expect to find offsets — small corms around the parent — which can be potted separately. Do not size up more than one pot at a time.

common_problems.problem: Leaves dropping one after another over winter
common_problems.fix: Dormancy. Alocasias often go down to nothing and come back in spring. Cut the water right back, keep the corm just barely damp, stop feeding, and wait. Throwing it out in February is the usual mistake.

common_problems.problem: Fine webbing, leaves going dull and stippled
common_problems.fix: Spider mites. This genus is their favourite. Shower the plant, wipe both sides of every leaf, and treat weekly for a month. Raise the humidity or they come straight back.

common_problems.problem: Yellow leaf with a brown mushy stem
common_problems.fix: Rot at the corm from a wet mix. Unpot immediately, cut back to firm white tissue, and repot into bark and perlite.

common_problems.problem: Dry brown patches in the middle of a leaf
common_problems.fix: Sunburn. Move it out of direct sun; the damage does not heal.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and people if chewed — the sap carries insoluble calcium oxalate crystals, which burn the mouth and throat. Keep it off the floor if anything in the house tastes its way through life.

card.summary: Taro: the elephant ear grown as a food crop across the tropics, with huge soft leaves held on drooping stems. Unlike every other aroid on this list it wants to be wet — it grows in paddies — and will happily sit in a saucer of standing water.
card.light: Bright light and happy in direct sun for part of the day — unlike its alocasia cousins, this is a marsh plant from open ground.
card.water: Keep it wet. Not damp — wet. A colocasia that dries out fully drops its leaves and may not come back. As a starting point, water every 4 days.
card.humidity: 60% and above, or spider mites will find it.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C) — colder than that and it dies back to the corm.
card.soil: The exception to every aroid drainage rule. Colocasia grows in standing water in the wild and is perfectly happy in a heavy, rich compost kept constantly damp, even in a saucer of water.
card.feeding: Balanced feed at half strength every second or third watering, spring through summer only.
card.repotting: Once a year in spring. Expect to find offsets — small corms around the parent — which can be potted separately. Do not size up more than one pot at a time.

card.summary: Angel wings: paper-thin leaves in pink, white, red and green, so translucent they light up from behind. It is a seasonal plant grown from a tuber — it leafs up in spring, performs all summer, then dies back completely in autumn and spends the winter as a dry tuber in its pot.
card.light: Bright indirect light — more than people give them. An alocasia in a dim room loses a leaf for every new one it makes and slowly winds down to nothing. Direct afternoon sun, though, burns holes in those thin leaves.
card.water: Keep evenly damp while it is in leaf, then stop completely once it starts to die back in autumn. As a starting point, water every 4 days.
card.humidity: 60% and up while in leaf.
card.temperature: Wants warmth: 70–85°F (21–29°C). Below about 60°F (15°C) it dies back to its tuber for the winter.
card.soil: Alocasias grow from a corm, and a corm sitting in wet compost rots. Use a very open mix and a pot with real drainage. Many growers keep them in semi-hydroponics for exactly this reason.
card.feeding: Balanced feed at half strength every second or third watering, spring through summer only.
card.repotting: Caladiums die back to the tuber every autumn. Keep the dry tuber in its pot somewhere warm over winter, stop watering entirely, and start again in spring — that is the plant's habit, not a failure.

card.summary: The ZZ plant: glossy, almost artificial-looking leaflets on upright stalks growing out of fat underground rhizomes that store water for months.
card.light: The ZZ plant handles more neglect and less light than anything else on this list. It grows faster in bright indirect light, but it will hold its looks for years in a corner that would kill a pothos.
card.water: Water when the pot is completely dry, and then not very much. Three weeks between drinks is normal; six is survivable. Wrinkling stems, not drooping ones, are the signal it is thirsty. As a starting point, water every 3 weeks.
card.humidity: Indifferent.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–85°F (15–29°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C). Ordinary room temperatures suit it fine.
card.soil: It stores water in potato-like rhizomes under the surface, so the mix must let go of water quickly. Cactus compost with a little extra perlite is ideal.
card.feeding: A weak feed two or three times over the whole growing season. It genuinely does not need much.
card.repotting: Every two or three years. You will know when the rhizomes start deforming the pot, which they do — plastic pots crack.

common_problems.problem: Yellow stems that go soft at the base
common_problems.fix: Overwatering. This is the only reliable way to kill a ZZ. Stop watering. Unpot, cut away any rotten rhizome, let the cut surfaces dry for a day, and repot in dry gritty mix.

common_problems.problem: Stems flopping outward from the centre
common_problems.fix: Too little light — it is reaching — or a pot that has become top-heavy. Move it brighter. Staking is a cosmetic fix; the light is the cause.

common_problems.problem: Dusty, dull leaves
common_problems.fix: Just dust. The waxy surface shows it. Wipe with a damp cloth. It improves the light reaching the plant more than people expect.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and people if chewed — the sap carries insoluble calcium oxalate crystals, which burn the mouth and throat. Keep it off the floor if anything in the house tastes its way through life.

card.summary: The peace lily: dark glossy leaves and white spathes on tall stems, sold as an easy low-light plant. It is easy, but 'low light' is the part that misleads people — it will live in a dim room and never flower there.
card.light: Medium to bright indirect light. Peace lilies are sold as low-light plants and will live in a dim room, but they will not flower there. A spot with bright light and no direct sun gives you both the leaves and the spathes.
card.water: Water when the top of the compost is dry. A peace lily dramatically collapses when thirsty and recovers within an hour of a drink — useful, but doing it repeatedly costs it leaves. As a starting point, water every 5 days.
card.humidity: Above 50% keeps the tips from browning.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C) — cold drafts brown and collapse the leaves.
card.soil: Ordinary peat-free compost with a third perlite. Peace lilies want moisture-retentive, not chunky — they are the least epiphytic aroid on this list.
card.feeding: Balanced feed at half strength monthly, spring to early autumn.
card.repotting: Every spring while young, then every other year. Divide the clump at the same time if it has outgrown its place.

common_problems.problem: Brown crispy leaf tips
common_problems.fix: Tap water minerals, over-feeding, or dry air — in that order of likelihood. Flush the pot with plain water, feed at half strength, and raise humidity.

common_problems.problem: Whole plant collapses
common_problems.fix: Dry. It is theatrical about this. Water thoroughly. If it collapses while the compost is wet, the roots have rotted and the cause is the opposite.

common_problems.problem: Green flowers instead of white
common_problems.fix: Too much fertiliser, or the spathe simply ageing. Cut the old spathes off at the base and ease off the feed.

common_problems.problem: No flowers at all
common_problems.fix: Not enough light. Move it to a brighter spot out of the sun and feed through spring.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and people if chewed — the sap carries insoluble calcium oxalate crystals, which burn the mouth and throat. Keep it off the floor if anything in the house tastes its way through life.

card.summary: Chinese evergreen: broad leaves marbled in silver, cream, pink or red on a short compact plant. The silver and green kinds are among the best genuinely low-light plants sold; the pink and red cultivars are a different proposition and need real brightness to keep their colour.
card.light: Medium indirect light suits the green and silver varieties, which is why they end up in offices. The pink, red and cream cultivars carry far less chlorophyll and need genuinely bright indirect light to keep their colour and keep growing.
card.water: Water when the top half of the pot is dry. Aglaonemas tolerate a missed week far better than an extra one. As a starting point, water every 9 days.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 60°F (15°C). Chilled leaves get dark, water-soaked patches.
card.soil: Ordinary potting compost with a third perlite. Aglaonemas are not fussy; they only object to sitting wet.
card.feeding: Balanced feed at half strength monthly in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every second or third spring. They are slow and are perfectly happy slightly potbound.

common_problems.problem: Yellow lower leaves
common_problems.fix: Overwatering, or cold. Let it dry further between waterings and keep it above 15 °C — they sulk in a draught.

common_problems.problem: Colour washing out of a pink or red variety
common_problems.fix: Not enough light. Move it brighter, out of direct sun.

common_problems.problem: Grey mushy patches after a cold spell
common_problems.fix: Cold damage. Remove the damaged leaves and move it away from the window or door that did it.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and people if chewed — the sap carries insoluble calcium oxalate crystals, which burn the mouth and throat. Keep it off the floor if anything in the house tastes its way through life.

card.summary: A compact aglaonema with green leaves edged and veined in hot pink-red, on pink stems. Like all the red and pink aglaonemas it needs more light than the silver kinds — the colour is what the extra light buys.

card.summary: Dumb cane: big paddle leaves splashed with cream, on a thick upright cane that goes bare at the bottom as it ages.

common_problems.problem: Leaning hard toward the window
common_problems.fix: Uneven light. Dieffenbachia grows toward it faster than most. Turn the pot a quarter turn every week.

common_problems.problem: Bare stem with a tuft of leaves on top
common_problems.fix: Normal ageing. Cut the crown off with 10 cm of stem and re-root it; the stump usually shoots again.

common_problems.problem: Yellow lower leaves
common_problems.fix: Overwatering, or cold water. Let it dry down further and use tepid water.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and people. The common name — dumb cane — comes from the effect of chewing it: the calcium oxalate crystals swell the mouth and tongue and can make speech and swallowing painful for days. Worth placing out of reach of small children.

card.summary: Arrowhead vine: it starts as a compact rosette of arrow-shaped leaves and then, given something to climb, turns into a vine with completely different lobed adult foliage. It grows fast, roots from anything, and comes in more colour forms than almost any other houseplant — pink, cream, speckled, near-white.
card.light: Bright indirect light. Plain green syngoniums manage in medium light; the pink, white and speckled cultivars lose their markings without a bright spot.
card.water: Water when the top third of the pot is dry. Philodendrons wilt visibly when genuinely thirsty and recover within hours, which makes them easy to read. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Fine at room humidity, faster growth above 60%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C); keep it above 60°F (15°C).
card.soil: Almost all of them climb or creep rather than sit in deep soil, so the roots want air. Half potting compost, half bark and perlite is the standard recipe. Crawlers like gloriosum want a shallow wide pot rather than a deep one — the rhizome runs along the surface.
card.feeding: Balanced liquid feed at half strength every third watering through the growing season.
card.repotting: Every spring while young — they grow fast. A syngonium that is allowed to climb changes leaf shape entirely, from the arrowhead most people know to a large lobed adult leaf.

common_problems.problem: Long bare stems with leaves far apart
common_problems.fix: Too little light. The plant is reaching. Move it brighter and cut the leggy growth back — it will branch from the nodes below the cut.

common_problems.problem: Yellow lower leaves
common_problems.fix: Usually overwatering; occasionally just age, one leaf at a time. If several go at once, check the roots. Brown and soft means rot; trim them and repot into fresh airy mix.

common_problems.problem: Variegation fading back to plain green
common_problems.fix: Not enough light for the plant to afford the white tissue. Give it more light, and prune back to a node that still shows variegation — the plant grows on from the last variegated point.

common_problems.problem: Brown tips on new leaves that were fine in the old pot
common_problems.fix: Low humidity while the leaf was still unfurling. Group plants together or run a humidifier while new leaves open; the damage is cosmetic and permanent on that leaf.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and people if chewed — the sap carries insoluble calcium oxalate crystals, which burn the mouth and throat. Keep it off the floor if anything in the house tastes its way through life.

card.summary: Mini monstera — which it isn't; it's neither a monstera nor a philodendron, despite being sold as both. A fast, slender climbing aroid with small deeply-split leaves, it grows several leaves a month in summer and is one of the quickest ways to get a green wall of fenestration in a small flat.
card.light: Bright indirect light. It is not a monstera and not a philodendron despite both nicknames, but it wants the same thing: bright light out of the sun's direct path, and something to climb.
card.water: Water when the top 5 cm of mix is dry, then water until it runs out of the bottom. Monsteras would rather be a day late than a day early. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Happy at normal room humidity; better above 50%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C) and out of cold drafts.
card.soil: Monsteras are climbers that root into bark in the wild, not into soil. A peat-only compost holds water against the roots and is the usual reason a healthy plant turns yellow. Cut potting soil half-and-half with orchid bark and perlite, or buy a ready-made aroid mix.
card.feeding: A balanced liquid feed at half strength, every second or third watering in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Repot when roots come out of the drainage holes, in spring. Go up one pot size only — a monstera in too big a pot sits wet. Give it a moss pole at the same time: aerial roots that find something to climb produce noticeably larger, better-fenestrated leaves.

common_problems.problem: Yellow leaves, usually the oldest ones first
common_problems.fix: Overwatering, or a mix that holds water. The roots have been wet long enough to start dying back. Let it dry out further between waterings, and repot into something chunkier if the mix stays soggy for days.

common_problems.problem: New leaves come out small and with no splits
common_problems.fix: Not enough light, or nothing to climb. Move it closer to the window and give it a moss pole. Fenestration is a maturity signal; the plant withholds it when conditions say stay small.

common_problems.problem: Brown crispy edges
common_problems.fix: Dry air, or a build-up of salts from tap water and fertiliser. Raise humidity, and flush the pot thoroughly with plain water every few months.

common_problems.problem: Fine webbing between stems, leaves stippled pale
common_problems.fix: Spider mites, which arrive in dry warm air. Shower the whole plant, then treat every five days for three weeks — one treatment never gets the eggs.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and people if chewed — the sap carries insoluble calcium oxalate crystals, which burn the mouth and throat. Keep it off the floor if anything in the house tastes its way through life.

card.summary: The shingle plant: small, round, dark-green leaves pressed flat against a board or bark as it climbs, overlapping like scales. It is grown entirely for that habit and usually sold mounted on a plank; without a flat surface to climb it trails and loses the look.
card.light: Bright indirect light. It is not a monstera and not a philodendron despite both nicknames, but it wants the same thing: bright light out of the sun's direct path, and something to climb.
card.water: Water when the top 5 cm of mix is dry, then water until it runs out of the bottom. Monsteras would rather be a day late than a day early. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Above 60%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C) and out of cold drafts.

card.repotting: Rarely — it usually lives on its mount. Keep the board or bark it climbs damp, and give it a taller one when it reaches the top.

card.summary: The fiddle-leaf fig: huge violin-shaped leaves on an upright trunk, and the most photographed and most complained-about houseplant of the last decade. It is not difficult so much as inflexible — it wants a bright spot, a steady routine, and to be left exactly where it is.
card.light: Bright light, and the more the better — several hours of direct morning sun suits them. These are canopy trees, not understorey plants, and the leggy, leaf-dropping ficus in a dim corner is the single most common indoor failure of the genus.
card.water: Water when the top 5 cm is dry, thoroughly, and empty the saucer. Ficus hate both extremes and will drop leaves to tell you about either. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Room humidity is adequate; above 50% reduces leaf drop.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–80°F (15–27°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C). Drafts and sudden changes are what make figs drop leaves.
card.soil: A loam-based compost (John Innes No. 2 or its equivalent) with perlite mixed through. Ficus want weight and structure around the roots rather than the airy mixes aroids like.
card.feeding: Balanced feed at half strength every two to four weeks in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every second or third spring, one size up. A ficus resents disturbance and will usually drop leaves after repotting — that is normal and passes in a month.

common_problems.problem: Leaves dropping after you moved it
common_problems.fix: Ficus dislike change — light, temperature, position, all of it. Put it somewhere bright and leave it there. Resist the urge to fix it; the drop stops within a few weeks.

common_problems.problem: Brown spots spreading from the leaf edges
common_problems.fix: Overwatering. The roots are suffocating. Let the top third dry out fully before the next water, and check the pot drains freely.

common_problems.problem: Bare lower stem, leaves only at the top
common_problems.fix: Not enough light. Move it into the brightest spot you have and prune the top back in spring — it branches from below the cut.

common_problems.problem: Sticky leaves and a black sooty film
common_problems.fix: Scale insects on the stems and leaf undersides. Scrape them off with a fingernail, then treat with horticultural soap every week for a month.

card.toxicity: Mildly toxic to cats and dogs. The milky sap irritates the mouth and stomach and can irritate skin on contact, so wear gloves when pruning.

card.summary: The dwarf umbrella tree: leaflets arranged in a wheel around the end of each stalk, on a plant that branches freely and takes hard pruning without complaint. It is fast, cheap, forgiving and one of the best value large green plants there is.
card.light: Bright indirect light with an hour or two of sun. In poor light the stems stretch and the plant leans; variegated forms lose their cream markings entirely.
card.water: Water when the top third is dry. More scheffleras are lost to a permanently wet pot than to drought. As a starting point, water every 8 days.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–80°F (15–27°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C).
card.soil: Ordinary potting compost with a third perlite. They are not particular, as long as the pot drains.
card.feeding: Balanced feed at half strength monthly through spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every second spring. Prune hard at the same time if it has gone lanky — scheffleras take it well and branch generously.

common_problems.problem: Leaves dropping in quantity
common_problems.fix: Usually overwatering, sometimes a cold draught. Check the pot is not sitting wet, and move it away from the door.

common_problems.problem: Long bare stems with a few leaves at the top
common_problems.fix: Too little light. Move it brighter and cut it back by a third in spring.

common_problems.problem: Sticky residue on the leaves below
common_problems.fix: Scale or mealybugs above. Check the leaf undersides and stem joints, wipe them off with alcohol on a cotton bud, and treat weekly for a month.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and people if chewed — the sap carries insoluble calcium oxalate crystals, which burn the mouth and throat. Keep it off the floor if anything in the house tastes its way through life.

card.summary: The snake plant — still called Sansevieria by almost everyone, though it was moved to Dracaena in 2017. Stiff upright leaves banded in grey-green, growing from a spreading rhizome.
card.light: Medium to bright indirect light. The snake plants in this genus tolerate deep shade and full sun alike, but the leafy dracaenas — marginata, fragrans, the rest — scorch in direct sun and stretch in the dark.
card.water: Let the top half of the pot dry out for the leafy kinds; let the whole pot dry for the snake plants. Both are far more often overwatered than under. As a starting point, water every 3 weeks.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C) and away from cold windows.
card.soil: Free-draining is the whole requirement. Ordinary compost cut with a third perlite for the leafy kinds; cactus compost for the snake plants, which rot at the base if the mix holds water.
card.feeding: A weak balanced feed monthly in spring and summer; none in winter.
card.repotting: Every two or three years. Snake plants flower and grow best slightly potbound, so leave them until the pot is visibly straining.

common_problems.problem: Brown tips on long thin leaves
common_problems.fix: Fluoride and salts in tap water — dracaenas are unusually sensitive. Water with rainwater or filtered water, and flush the pot through a few times a year.

common_problems.problem: Soft yellow base on a snake plant, leaves falling out of the pot
common_problems.fix: Rot. Water has sat in the crown or the mix. Take the firm leaves as cuttings and start again. Water snake plants from below or around the edge, never into the centre.

common_problems.problem: Lower leaves yellowing and dropping on a cane dracaena
common_problems.fix: Normal ageing if it is one at a time; overwatering if it is several. Peel the old leaves off cleanly and check the mix is drying out between waterings.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs. The saponins cause vomiting, drooling and — in cats specifically — dilated pupils. Not dangerous to people beyond an upset stomach.

card.summary: The dragon tree: thin arching leaves edged in red on top of slender grey canes, often several canes of different heights in one pot. It is slow, tough, and unusually sensitive to fluoride — the brown leaf tips almost every specimen has are usually the tap water, not you.
card.light: Medium to bright indirect light. The snake plants in this genus tolerate deep shade and full sun alike, but the leafy dracaenas — marginata, fragrans, the rest — scorch in direct sun and stretch in the dark.
card.water: Let the top half of the pot dry out for the leafy kinds; let the whole pot dry for the snake plants. Both are far more often overwatered than under. As a starting point, water every 10 days.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C) and away from cold windows.
card.soil: Free-draining is the whole requirement. Ordinary compost cut with a third perlite for the leafy kinds; cactus compost for the snake plants, which rot at the base if the mix holds water.
card.feeding: A weak balanced feed monthly in spring and summer; none in winter.
card.repotting: Every two or three years. Snake plants flower and grow best slightly potbound, so leave them until the pot is visibly straining.

card.summary: Lucky bamboo: the upright or spiralled green stems sold standing in a vase of pebbles and water. It is not a bamboo — it is a dracaena, in the asparagus family, and the resemblance is only in the jointed stem.
card.light: Bright indirect light, and never direct sun — the leaves of a plant grown in water scorch faster than one in compost. It survives a dim corner, but pales and stops putting out new leaves.
card.water: Grown in water: keep the roots covered, change the water every week or two, and use rainwater, filtered or tap water left standing overnight. It is unusually sensitive to the fluoride and chlorine in fresh tap water, which shows as burnt tips. Grown in compost: keep it evenly damp, and let only the top centimetre dry. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C) and away from cold windows.

card.summary: The spineless yucca: thick woody canes topped with fountains of sword-shaped leaves, sold as sawn-off logs that sprout. It wants the sunniest spot in the house and almost no water — indoors it is nearly always overwatered, and the base goes soft long before the top shows anything.
card.light: Full sun. A yucca indoors wants the brightest window in the house and will stretch and weaken anywhere else.
card.water: Water when the pot is completely dry, and sparingly in winter. A yucca will go a month without complaint. As a starting point, water every 2 weeks.
card.humidity: Indifferent; dry air suits it.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–80°F (15–27°C) and tolerant of a cool room; keep it above 45°F (7°C).
card.soil: Cactus compost, or ordinary compost cut with a third horticultural grit. The cane rots quickly in anything that holds water.
card.feeding: A weak feed two or three times a year, no more.
card.repotting: Every three years or so. They are top-heavy — use a wide, weighted pot.

common_problems.problem: Soft brown base, leaves pulling away
common_problems.fix: Rot from overwatering. Cut the cane back above the rot, let it callus for a few days, and re-root it in dry gritty mix.

common_problems.problem: Leaves going pale and floppy
common_problems.fix: Not enough light. Move it to the sunniest window you have.

common_problems.problem: Brown leaf tips
common_problems.fix: Dry air or fluoride in tap water. Trim them at an angle with scissors and switch to rainwater.

card.toxicity: Mildly toxic to cats and dogs; the saponins cause vomiting. The leaf tips are sharp enough to be the greater hazard with small children.

card.summary: The money tree: several young trunks braided together while soft, topped with palmate leaves of five to seven leaflets. It is a swamp tree in the wild, which is why it tolerates a heavier pot than most, and it is one of very few larger houseplants that is completely non-toxic to cats and dogs.
card.light: Bright indirect light. Direct midday sun scorches the leaflets; deep shade makes the stems stretch and the braid open up.
card.water: Water thoroughly when the top half of the pot is dry, then let it drain completely. Every week or two is typical indoors. As a starting point, water every 8 days.
card.humidity: Above 50% is appreciated.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C) and out of drafts.
card.soil: Ordinary compost with a third perlite or coarse sand. The swollen trunk stores water, so the mix must not.
card.feeding: Balanced feed at half strength monthly in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every second or third spring. Braided specimens are several young trees planted together — they can be separated at repotting if you would rather have one proper tree.

common_problems.problem: Yellow leaves dropping from the bottom
common_problems.fix: Overwatering. The trunk is a reservoir and does not need help. Water less often and make sure the pot is not standing in water.

common_problems.problem: Leaflets going brown and crisp at the edges
common_problems.fix: Dry air. Raise the humidity — group it with other plants or run a humidifier.

common_problems.problem: The braid loosening and stems going bare
common_problems.fix: Too little light. Move it brighter and prune the tops back in spring to force branching.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs, and one of the few larger houseplants that is.

card.summary: The jade plant: fat glossy oval leaves on a thickening woody trunk, slowly becoming a miniature tree. Given full sun and very little water it lives for decades and takes on red-edged leaves and a genuinely gnarled shape.
card.light: Four to six hours of direct sun. A jade in a dim room stretches into a thin pale thing that never regains its compact shape.
card.water: Water thoroughly, then not again until the pot is bone dry and the leaves have lost a little of their firmness. In winter, once a month is plenty. As a starting point, water every 2 weeks.
card.humidity: Indifferent; dry air is fine.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C). A cool winter around 50–55°F (10–13°C) helps it flower; keep it above 40°F (4°C) and frost-free.
card.soil: Cactus compost, ideally with more grit still. The one thing a jade cannot survive is a mix that stays damp.
card.feeding: A weak cactus feed two or three times over the summer.
card.repotting: Every three or four years, and into a heavy pot — a mature jade is top-heavy and a plastic pot will tip.

common_problems.problem: Leaves dropping at a touch
common_problems.fix: Overwatering, almost always. Stop watering until the pot is fully dry, then water far less often.

common_problems.problem: Stretched pale stems with leaves far apart
common_problems.fix: Not enough light. Move it into direct sun and cut the stretched growth back — the cuttings will root.

common_problems.problem: Red edges on the leaves
common_problems.fix: Sun and cool nights. This is a good sign, not a problem. Nothing to fix; it is the plant colouring up.

common_problems.problem: White cottony spots in the leaf joints
common_problems.fix: Mealybugs. Dab each one with alcohol on a cotton bud and check again weekly for a month.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs; causes vomiting and lethargy. Not a hazard to people.

card.summary: The ponytail palm — neither a palm nor a tree, but a member of the asparagus family with a swollen water-storing base and a fountain of thin strappy leaves. It is the most drought-tolerant plant in this catalogue after the lithops: a month without water is routine.
card.light: Full sun. A yucca indoors wants the brightest window in the house and will stretch and weaken anywhere else.
card.water: Water thoroughly, then leave it until the pot is completely dry — the swollen base is a water tank and a ponytail palm is happy forgotten for a month. As a starting point, water every 2 weeks.
card.humidity: Indifferent; dry air suits it.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–85°F (15–29°C) and fine with a cool winter; keep it above 45°F (7°C).
card.soil: Cactus compost, or ordinary compost cut with a third horticultural grit. The cane rots quickly in anything that holds water.
card.feeding: A weak feed two or three times a year, no more.
card.repotting: Every three years or so. They are top-heavy — use a wide, weighted pot.

common_problems.problem: Soft, squashy base
common_problems.fix: Rot. It has been watered too often. Cut away the rot if any firm tissue remains, dry it out, and repot in gritty mix. Often fatal — prevention is the only real answer.

common_problems.problem: Brown leaf tips
common_problems.fix: Dry air or salts building up. Trim the tips and flush the pot with plain water occasionally.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs.

card.summary: Ming aralia: finely divided lacy foliage on twisting woody stems, slow-growing and sculptural, and a traditional bonsai subject. It is the fussiest plant in this section — it drops its leaves at any change and wants humidity above 60% — but a settled one is beautiful and very long-lived.
card.light: Bright indirect light. Aralias drop leaves when they are moved, when it gets cold, and when the light changes — a stable bright position matters more than an ideal one.
card.water: Keep evenly damp, never soggy, and never let it dry out completely — an aralia that dries hard defoliates. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Above 60%. This is a genuinely humidity-hungry plant.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 60°F (15°C). Drafts and cold make it drop leaves.
card.soil: Ordinary compost with a third perlite. They want steady moisture without sitting wet.
card.feeding: Balanced feed at half strength monthly in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every second or third spring; they are slow and dislike disturbance. Expect leaf drop afterwards.

common_problems.problem: Sudden leaf drop
common_problems.fix: A change: a move, a draught, a cold night, or the compost drying out. Put it somewhere stable and bright, keep it evenly damp, and be patient.

common_problems.problem: Spider mites
common_problems.fix: Dry air. Aralias attract them reliably. Raise humidity and treat weekly for a month.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs — the saponins cause vomiting and mouth irritation.

card.summary: The shield aralia, often sold as 'Fabian': round, glossy, dark-green leaves, purple underneath, on thick upright stems. A much easier aralia than the Ming, though it still drops leaves when it is moved or chilled.
card.light: Bright indirect light. Aralias drop leaves when they are moved, when it gets cold, and when the light changes — a stable bright position matters more than an ideal one.
card.water: Keep evenly damp, never soggy, and never let it dry out completely — an aralia that dries hard defoliates. As a starting point, water weekly.

card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 60°F (15°C). Drafts and cold make it drop leaves.

card.repotting: Every second or third spring; they are slow and dislike disturbance. Expect leaf drop afterwards.

common_problems.fix: Dry air. Aralias attract them reliably. Raise humidity and treat weekly for a month.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs — the saponins cause vomiting and mouth irritation.

card.summary: Japanese aralia: big glossy hand-shaped leaves on a shrubby plant that is hardy outdoors in mild climates. Indoors it wants a cool, bright, shaded spot — a hallway or a cold porch suits it far better than a heated living room, which is the opposite of most of this list.
card.light: Medium indirect light and, unusually, a cool room. Fatsia is hardy outdoors in mild climates and struggles in a hot dry lounge more than in a chilly hallway.
card.water: Keep evenly damp through spring and summer, drier in winter. Wilting leaves recover, but the leaf edges brown permanently. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Above 50%.
card.temperature: Prefers it cool: 50–70°F (10–21°C). One of the few houseplants happier in a cool room than a warm one; fine down to 40°F (4°C).
card.soil: A loam-based compost that holds some water. Fatsia is not a plant that wants to dry out.
card.feeding: Balanced feed monthly in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every second spring. It grows fast and gets large; prune in spring to keep it in bounds.

common_problems.problem: Yellow leaves with brown edges
common_problems.fix: Too warm and too dry. Move it somewhere cooler, raise humidity, keep the compost damp.

common_problems.problem: Spider mites in a warm room
common_problems.fix: Dry heat. Shower the plant and treat weekly; a cooler spot is the real cure.

common_problems.problem: Pale washed-out leaves
common_problems.fix: Too much direct sun. Move it into shade.

card.toxicity: Mildly toxic to cats and dogs — causes vomiting if chewed.

card.summary: The giant white bird of paradise: enormous paddle leaves on tall stems, forming a fan several metres across. It is grown indoors for the architecture, not the flowers — almost none flower in a living room.
card.light: As much light as possible, including direct sun. A bird of paradise will not flower in anything less, and indoors most never do — treat the leaves as the point and any flower as a bonus.
card.water: Water thoroughly when the top third is dry. They drink hard in summer and much less in winter. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C).
card.soil: A rich loam-based compost with perlite or grit. These are big hungry plants with thick fleshy roots that still resent standing water.
card.feeding: A balanced feed every two weeks through spring and summer — they are heavy feeders.
card.repotting: Every second spring while young, then leave it: strelitzias flower better potbound, and a mature one is heavy enough that top-dressing is the practical option.

common_problems.problem: Leaves splitting along the ribs
common_problems.fix: Normal. The splits let wind through in the wild. Nothing to fix. Splits appear faster in a draught or when the leaves rub against something.

common_problems.problem: No flowers after years indoors
common_problems.fix: Not enough light, too much pot, or simply not old enough — they flower at four or five years. Give it the sunniest position you have, feed through summer, and stop repotting.

common_problems.problem: Brown crispy leaf edges
common_problems.fix: Under-watering or salt build-up. Water more thoroughly and flush the pot a few times a year.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs — the seeds and flowers most of all. Causes vomiting and drowsiness.

card.summary: The orange bird of paradise: smaller and stiffer than nicolai, with grey-green paddle leaves and — given enough sun and enough age — the famous orange and blue crane-headed flower. It needs four or five years and the brightest window in the house before it will bloom.
card.light: As much light as possible, including direct sun. A bird of paradise will not flower in anything less, and indoors most never do — treat the leaves as the point and any flower as a bonus.
card.water: Water thoroughly when the top third is dry. They drink hard in summer and much less in winter. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C).
card.soil: A rich loam-based compost with perlite or grit. These are big hungry plants with thick fleshy roots that still resent standing water.
card.feeding: A balanced feed every two weeks through spring and summer — they are heavy feeders.
card.repotting: Every second spring while young, then leave it: strelitzias flower better potbound, and a mature one is heavy enough that top-dressing is the practical option.

common_problems.fix: Normal. The splits let wind through in the wild. Nothing to fix. Splits appear faster in a draught or when the leaves rub against something.

common_problems.fix: Not enough light, too much pot, or simply not old enough — they flower at four or five years. Give it the sunniest position you have, feed through summer, and stop repotting.

common_problems.problem: Brown crispy leaf edges
common_problems.fix: Under-watering or salt build-up. Water more thoroughly and flush the pot a few times a year.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs — the seeds and flowers most of all. Causes vomiting and drowsiness.

card.summary: The dwarf banana: huge soft paddle leaves that unfurl from a central spear, growing at a speed that has to be seen to be believed in a warm bright room. It is greedy, thirsty, short-lived and constantly producing pups — treat the parent as temporary and the pups as the plant.
card.light: As much direct sun as you can manage. Bananas are field crops; indoors they want the brightest window there is.
card.water: Keep the compost damp at all times in summer — near-daily watering in a warm room is normal. Ease off in winter. As a starting point, water every 4 days.
card.humidity: Above 60%, or the leaf edges brown.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C). Cold stops growth and scorches the leaves.
card.soil: A rich compost that holds water. Bananas are greedy and thirsty and will not be talked out of it.
card.feeding: A high-nitrogen feed every week or two in summer.
card.repotting: Every spring — they grow astonishingly fast and exhaust their compost within a season.

common_problems.problem: Brown crispy leaf edges
common_problems.fix: Dry air, almost always. Raise the humidity. Some edge browning on indoor bananas is unavoidable.

common_problems.problem: Leaves tearing into strips
common_problems.fix: Normal for the genus, and worse in a draught. Nothing to fix; move it out of the airflow if it bothers you.

common_problems.problem: Growth stalling in a warm bright spot
common_problems.fix: Hungry or potbound. Feed weekly and repot — bananas outgrow pots in a single season.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs.

card.summary: The Norfolk Island pine: not a true pine but a conifer from a small Pacific island, with soft, tiered branches of short needles. Sold everywhere as a living Christmas tree, it will grow for decades indoors in a bright, cool room — but it loses lower branches in the dark, and they never grow back.
card.light: Bright light, and some direct sun if you have it. A Norfolk Island pine in a dim room drops its lower branches one tier at a time, and they never grow back.
card.water: Water when the top few centimetres are dry, thoroughly, and empty the saucer. Less in winter, but never let the pot dry right out. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Above 50%; dry winter heat browns the needles.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–75°F (15–24°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C). A cool, bright room suits it better than a warm, dark one.
card.soil: Ordinary peat-free compost cut with a third grit or perlite. It wants steady moisture, but the roots rot in a mix that stays wet.
card.feeding: A balanced feed at half strength monthly in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every three or four years, in spring. It grows slowly in a pot and is happy a little tight.

common_problems.problem: Lower branches turning brown and dropping
common_problems.fix: Not enough light, or the compost dried out. Move it into the brightest spot you have and keep the watering steady. Lost branches don't regrow, so it is worth catching early.

common_problems.problem: Needles browning at the tips
common_problems.fix: Dry air, usually from heating. Raise the humidity and keep it away from radiators.

common_problems.problem: Leaning toward the window
common_problems.fix: It grows toward the light. Turn the pot a quarter turn every week.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs.

card.summary: The olive tree: narrow grey-green leaves on twisting branches, now sold everywhere as an indoor tree. It is a sun plant that needs the brightest window you have and dry roots — and indoors it rarely fruits without a cold winter rest.
card.light: Full sun, as much as you can give it. An olive is a Mediterranean tree: indoors it needs a south-facing window or a summer outside, and in a dim room it drops its leaves.
card.water: Water thoroughly when the top half of the pot is dry. Olives would much rather be dry than wet, and need far less in winter. As a starting point, water every 10 days.
card.humidity: Indifferent; dry air suits it.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–80°F (15–27°C) in summer; a winter rest at 40–55°F (4–13°C) is what makes it flower.
card.soil: A loam-based compost with plenty of grit, in a pot that drains well. Olives put up with poor soil and drought, never with wet roots.
card.feeding: A balanced feed monthly from spring to late summer.
card.repotting: Every two or three years in spring, into a heavy pot — an olive in a light pot topples once it has a canopy.

common_problems.problem: Leaves dropping in winter
common_problems.fix: Too little light, especially in a warm room. Give it the brightest window — and a cooler spot in winter if you can, which is when it rests.

common_problems.problem: Leaves yellowing in a wet pot
common_problems.fix: Overwatering. Let it dry out well between waterings and check the pot drains.

common_problems.problem: Never flowers or fruits indoors
common_problems.fix: It needs a cold winter rest to set flowers. A few weeks below about 10 °C in winter — an unheated porch, say — is what most indoor olives are missing.

card.toxicity: Not on the ASPCA's list of toxic or non-toxic plants, so we don't call it pet-safe: not being listed is not the same as being tested. Keep it out of reach of a pet that chews.

card.summary: The parlour palm — named for the Victorian drawing rooms it survived, on gaslight and coal dust. Slender green canes with soft arching fronds, tolerant of low light and cool rooms, and non-toxic to cats and dogs.
card.light: Medium indirect light, and genuinely tolerant of less — the parlour palm earned its name in Victorian drawing rooms lit by gaslight. Direct sun scorches it.
card.water: Keep the top of the compost just barely damp. Palms will not forgive a pot left standing in water, and brown tips are the receipt for the one time you let it dry out hard. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Above 50% keeps the tips green.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C).
card.soil: Ordinary peat-free compost with perlite through it. Palms want moisture-retentive but never waterlogged.
card.feeding: A weak balanced feed monthly in spring and summer only.
card.repotting: Every two or three years, and reluctantly — palm roots resent disturbance. What is sold as one plant is usually a dozen seedlings in a pot; keep them together.

common_problems.problem: Brown tips on every frond
common_problems.fix: Dry air, hard tap water, or a dry spell. Almost universal indoors. Raise humidity, water with rainwater, and trim the brown off with scissors following the leaf's own shape.

common_problems.problem: Spider mites
common_problems.fix: Dry warm air. Palms are a favourite. Shower the fronds, both sides, and treat weekly for a month.

common_problems.problem: Whole fronds yellowing from the bottom
common_problems.fix: Normal ageing if one at a time; overwatering if several. Cut old fronds off at the base and check the mix is not staying wet.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs.

card.light: Bright light — far more than a parlour palm wants. Majesty palms are sold as low-light plants and slowly decline in them: the fronds thin and yellow, and the plant never fills back in.
card.water: Keep the compost consistently damp. Unusually for a palm it is a riverbank plant in the wild and wants it, but it still must not stand in water. As a starting point, water every 5 days.
card.humidity: Above 50%; dry air brings spider mites.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C).

card.summary: The fishtail palm: fronds divided into ragged, triangular leaflets shaped like a fish's tail fin, on a clump of several stems. Each stem flowers once and then dies, but the clump carries on.
card.light: Bright indirect light. Fishtail palms want more light than a parlour palm and thin out in a dim room.
card.water: Keep the compost evenly damp; the ragged leaflets brown quickly if it dries out. As a starting point, water every 6 days.
card.humidity: Above 50% keeps the tips green.

card.summary: The sago palm, which is not a palm at all but a cycad, from a group of plants older than the dinosaurs. A stiff crown of glossy, feathery fronds rises from a stout trunk, a single flush a year at most.
card.light: Bright light, with a few hours of direct sun if you can give it. A sago in a dim room puts out few, weak, stretched fronds — and it only makes a flush or two a year to begin with.
card.water: Water thoroughly when the top half of the pot has dried out, and much less in winter. Keep water out of the crown at the top of the trunk. As a starting point, water every 2 weeks.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–85°F (15–29°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C).
card.soil: Cactus or palm compost with extra grit or perlite. The stout trunk and thick roots store water, and a mix that stays wet rots them.
card.feeding: A palm feed with micronutrients two or three times in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every three years or so, and only when the roots fill the pot — it grows slowly and likes a snug pot. Keep the trunk at the depth it was; buried deeper, it rots.

common_problems.problem: The oldest ring of fronds turning yellow
common_problems.fix: Normal ageing if it is only the oldest fronds; overwatering if new ones yellow too. Cut old fronds off close to the trunk once they are fully yellow, and let the mix dry further between waterings.

common_problems.problem: New fronds come out pale, stunted or frizzled
common_problems.fix: Too little light, or a shortage of manganese — sagos are known for it. Move it brighter, and feed with a palm fertiliser that contains micronutrients.

common_problems.problem: Soft, rotting trunk at the base
common_problems.fix: Overwatering, or a trunk planted too deep. Unpot it, cut away soft tissue if it is limited, and replant at the right depth in gritty mix. A trunk that is soft right through can't be saved.

common_problems.problem: Small brown or white bumps on the fronds
common_problems.fix: Scale insects; sagos are prone to them. Scrape off what you can and treat with horticultural oil or soap every week for a month.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and people, and seriously so: every part is poisonous, the seeds most of all. Chewing it can cause vomiting, liver failure and death in dogs and cats. If a pet has eaten any, call a vet or animal poison line straight away rather than waiting for symptoms.

card.summary: The wax plant: thick leathery leaves on woody vines, and — given enough light and enough patience — umbels of star-shaped flowers that smell of chocolate at night and drip nectar onto whatever is underneath.
card.light: Bright indirect light, and a couple of hours of direct morning sun if you want flowers. Hoyas grown in medium light stay alive and green for years without ever blooming.
card.water: Water thoroughly when the pot is nearly dry and the leaves have just started to feel less firm. Hoyas store water in their leaves and are far more tolerant of drought than of wet feet. As a starting point, water every 10 days.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine; above 60% speeds growth.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C).
card.soil: Hoyas are epiphytes that root into bark and moss. A chunky mix of bark and perlite with a little compost is right; ordinary potting soil holds far too much water.
card.feeding: A balanced feed at half strength every second or third watering in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Rarely. Hoyas flower best tightly potbound, and repotting a plant that is about to bloom usually costs you the flowers. Every three or four years is plenty.

common_problems.problem: Never flowers
common_problems.fix: Not enough light, too much pot, or the flower spurs were cut off. Move it brighter, stop repotting, and never cut the old flower stalks — hoyas bloom from the same short spurs year after year.

common_problems.problem: Wrinkled, dimpled leaves
common_problems.fix: Under-watering — or, confusingly, root rot, which stops the plant drinking. Check the roots. Firm white roots mean water it; brown mushy roots mean repot and cut the damage away.

common_problems.problem: Yellow leaves dropping
common_problems.fix: Overwatering or cold. Let it dry out further and keep it above 15 °C.

common_problems.problem: Sticky black film under the flowers
common_problems.fix: The flowers themselves drip nectar; it is not a pest. Wipe it off. Put a saucer under a plant that is blooming heavily.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs, though the milky sap can irritate skin.

card.feeding: A balanced feed at half strength monthly in spring and summer.

common_problems.fix: It dried out. Water more often; tradescantias are thirstier than they look.

common_problems.fix: The compost stayed wet. Let it dry between waterings, and make sure the pot drains.

common_problems.problem: Brown leaf tips
common_problems.fix: Dry air, or salts from tap water. Raise the humidity and flush the pot through now and then.

card.toxicity: Mildly toxic to cats and dogs; the sap can also cause a skin rash in people who handle it a lot.

card.summary: Turtle vine: tiny, fleshy, oval leaves, often purple underneath, on stems that trail and creep into a dense mat. Fast and easy, and good spilling from a shelf or as ground cover in a large pot.
card.light: Bright indirect light. Turtle vine forms a dense mat of tiny leaves that thins and stretches in a dim spot.
card.water: Keep the compost lightly damp. It wilts fast and recovers fast, but repeated wilting costs it the lower leaves. As a starting point, water every 5 days.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–80°F (15–27°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C).
card.soil: Ordinary potting compost with perlite. Tradescantias are unfussy and grow at a speed that makes the mix almost irrelevant.
card.feeding: A balanced feed at half strength monthly in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every spring, or simply start again from cuttings — a tradescantia is at its best in its first year and goes bare in the middle in its second.

common_problems.problem: Bare leggy stems with leaves only at the ends
common_problems.fix: Normal growth habit plus too little light. Pinch the tips out regularly and root the cuttings back into the same pot. Move it brighter.

common_problems.problem: Stripes fading to green
common_problems.fix: Not enough light. Move it brighter and cut out any wholly green stems — they outgrow the variegated ones.

common_problems.problem: Brown crisp leaves
common_problems.fix: It dried out. Water more often; tradescantias are thirstier than they look.

card.toxicity: Mildly toxic to cats and dogs; the sap can also cause a skin rash in people who handle it a lot.

card.summary: Swedish ivy — neither Swedish nor an ivy, but a fast, trailing relative of mint with round, scalloped, glossy leaves and spikes of small white flowers. An old-fashioned and very easy hanging-basket plant.
card.light: Bright indirect light, with a little morning sun. Swedish ivy stretches and drops its lower leaves in a dim spot.
card.water: Keep the compost lightly damp, letting the top centimetre or two dry between waterings. As a starting point, water every 6 days.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–80°F (15–27°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C).
card.soil: Ordinary potting compost with some perlite. It is a fast, forgiving plant.
card.feeding: A balanced feed at half strength monthly in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every spring, or restart it from cuttings once it gets leggy.

common_problems.problem: Long bare stems
common_problems.fix: Not enough light, and no pinching. Pinch the tips regularly to make it branch, and move it brighter.

common_problems.problem: Wilting and dropping leaves
common_problems.fix: It dried out — or it sits wet. Check the compost: water if it is dry, let it drain if it is soggy.

common_problems.problem: White cottony blobs in the leaf joints
common_problems.fix: Mealybugs. Dab them with alcohol on a cotton bud every few days for a month.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs.

card.summary: The spider plant: arching striped leaves and long runners carrying miniature plantlets — the babies that made it the most-shared houseplant in the world. Its thick white roots store water, so it forgives a missed fortnight, and the brown tips nearly every specimen has are usually fluoride in the tap water.
card.light: Bright indirect light. Spider plants cope with less but produce fewer runners, and the variegation is sharpest in a bright spot out of direct sun.
card.water: Keep lightly damp in summer, drier in winter. They store water in the roots and survive a missed fortnight. As a starting point, water every 6 days.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 55–80°F (13–27°C) and tolerant of a cool room; keep it above 45°F (7°C).
card.soil: Ordinary compost with perlite. Spider plants build thick white water-storing roots that will crack a pot when they run out of room.
card.feeding: A balanced feed at half strength monthly in spring and summer; over-feeding causes brown tips.
card.repotting: Every spring while young. A spider plant that is not producing babies is usually one that needs a bigger pot — or, occasionally, one that needs a smaller one, since they flower when snug.

common_problems.problem: Brown tips on most leaves
common_problems.fix: Fluoride and salts in tap water — the classic spider plant complaint. Switch to rainwater or filtered water, flush the pot occasionally, and feed less.

common_problems.problem: Pale limp leaves
common_problems.fix: Too much direct sun. Move it out of the sun's direct path.

common_problems.problem: No babies
common_problems.fix: Too young, too dark, or too much pot. Give it a bright spot and leave it slightly potbound.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs. Cats are unusually drawn to chewing the leaves, which is hard on the plant — and a lot of any plant can still upset a cat's stomach.

card.summary: English ivy: the hardy climber from European woodland, sold indoors in dozens of leaf shapes and variegations. It is easy outdoors and awkward indoors, because central heating gives it spider mites within weeks.
card.light: Bright indirect light and, importantly, a cool room. Ivy is a hardy outdoor plant and does badly in dry central heating — a chilly porch suits it better than a warm lounge.
card.water: Keep evenly damp. Ivy dislikes drying out completely and shows it by browning from the tips back. As a starting point, water every 6 days.
card.humidity: Above 50%; dry heat brings spider mites.
card.temperature: Prefers it cool: 50–70°F (10–21°C). Cold isn't the risk — a warm, dry room is, because that is where spider mites thrive.
card.soil: Ordinary compost with perlite. Ivy is not fussy about the mix, only about the air around it.
card.feeding: A balanced feed at half strength monthly in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every second spring. Trim it hard at the same time; ivy takes cutting back well.

common_problems.problem: Spider mites, repeatedly
common_problems.fix: Warm dry air. Indoor ivy is a magnet for them. Move it somewhere cooler and more humid, shower it regularly, and treat weekly for a month when they appear.

common_problems.problem: Leaves going dry and brown from the edges
common_problems.fix: Dry heat or a pot that dried out. Water more regularly and move it away from the radiator.

common_problems.problem: Variegated ivy turning plain green
common_problems.fix: Too little light. Move it brighter and remove all-green shoots.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and people — causes vomiting and, on contact, a skin rash in some people.

card.summary: String of pearls: strands of spherical leaves, each with a translucent window along one side that lets light into the interior — an adaptation to reduce surface area in a dry climate. It has shallow fine roots and a deep pot of wet compost is the standard way it dies.
card.light: Bright light with a few hours of direct sun. Too dark, and string plants stretch into bare threads with the leaves far apart.
card.water: Water thoroughly when the pot is completely dry and the leaves have just started to look slightly flat or wrinkled. Every two to three weeks in summer, monthly in winter. As a starting point, water every 2 weeks.
card.humidity: Indifferent; dry air suits it.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C) while growing and fine a little cooler in winter; keep it above 50°F (10°C).
card.soil: Cactus compost with more perlite still, in a shallow pot. The swollen leaves are water stores and the roots are fine and shallow — depth of wet compost below them is what kills these plants.
card.feeding: A weak cactus feed two or three times over the summer.
card.repotting: Every two or three years, into a shallow wide pot rather than a deep one.

common_problems.problem: Shrivelled, flattened leaves
common_problems.fix: Thirsty — or rotting roots that can no longer take water up. Check the roots before you water. Firm roots mean it needs a drink; mushy ones mean rot.

common_problems.problem: Bare strings with leaves only at the ends
common_problems.fix: Too little light. Move it into direct sun and cut the bare strings back; they will branch.

common_problems.problem: Mushy stems at soil level
common_problems.fix: Rot from overwatering. Take healthy strand cuttings and start again.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and people; causes vomiting and, on contact, skin irritation.

card.summary: String of bananas: trailing stems lined with small, curved, banana-shaped leaves. Faster and more forgiving than string of pearls — less prone to rot, and quicker to recover from a missed watering.
card.light: Bright light with a few hours of direct sun. Too dark, and string plants stretch into bare threads with the leaves far apart.
card.water: Water thoroughly when the pot is completely dry and the leaves have just started to look slightly flat or wrinkled. Every two to three weeks in summer, monthly in winter. As a starting point, water every 12 days.

card.summary: String of hearts: fine purple strands of small marbled heart-shaped leaves, growing from a tuber. It makes small round tubers along the strands too, which makes it one of the easiest plants to propagate — press one onto compost and it roots.
