card.toxicity: Not on the ASPCA's list of toxic or non-toxic plants, so we don't call it pet-safe: not being listed is not the same as being tested. Keep it out of reach of a pet that chews.

card.summary: String of turtles: tiny round leaves patterned like a turtle's shell, on slow trailing stems. It is a peperomia rather than a succulent, so it wants more humidity and less sun than the other string plants — and it is very slow, so a full pot is worth paying for.
card.light: Bright indirect light, no direct sun. Peperomias are small understorey plants with thick leaves — they burn easily and stretch in the dark.
card.water: Let the top half of the pot dry out, then water thoroughly. The leaves store water — a peperomia would much rather be dry. As a starting point, water every 9 days.
card.humidity: Above 60%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C) and off cold windowsills in winter.
card.soil: Peperomias have small, shallow root systems and semi-succulent leaves. A light, airy mix in a small pot is the whole secret; a big pot of wet compost is the whole problem.
card.feeding: A weak balanced feed monthly in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Rarely, and into a pot barely bigger than the last. Peperomias are happiest tight.

common_problems.problem: Leaves dropping at a touch
common_problems.fix: Overwatering. Let it dry down properly and consider a smaller pot.

common_problems.problem: Leaves going soft and translucent
common_problems.fix: Rot, or cold water. Unpot and check the roots; use tepid water and keep it above 15 °C.

common_problems.problem: Stretched pale growth
common_problems.fix: Not enough light. Move it brighter, out of the sun's direct path.

card.toxicity: Not on the ASPCA's list itself, only its relatives, so we don't call it pet-safe. Keep it out of reach of a pet that chews.

card.summary: Also sold as rainbow peperomia: thick oval leaves edged in cream and rose over mid-green. It is a sport of the baby rubber plant and wants the same treatment — small pot, bright indirect light, and much less water than you would think.
card.light: Bright indirect light, no direct sun. Peperomias are small understorey plants with thick leaves — they burn easily and stretch in the dark.
card.water: Let the top half of the pot dry out, then water thoroughly. The leaves store water — a peperomia would much rather be dry. As a starting point, water every 9 days.

card.summary: A trailing hybrid with small, round, thick leaves set in threes and fours along its stems. Slow, compact, and very forgiving of a missed watering — the leaves are little water stores.
card.light: Bright indirect light, no direct sun. Peperomias are small understorey plants with thick leaves — they burn easily and stretch in the dark.
card.water: Let the top half of the pot dry out, then water thoroughly. The leaves store water — a peperomia would much rather be dry. As a starting point, water every 10 days.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine for most; the trailing kinds prefer above 60%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C) and off cold windowsills in winter.

card.summary: Rex begonia vine: velvety leaves quilted in silver, green and deep pink with red undersides, on a fast climbing vine with curling tendrils. It looks like a begonia and is actually a grape relative.
card.light: Bright indirect light, no direct sun. This is a jungle vine and the leaves mark easily.
card.water: Keep evenly damp. It wilts dramatically when dry and the leaves often do not fully recover. As a starting point, water every 5 days.
card.humidity: Above 60%. It will not thrive in dry air, full stop.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–80°F (15–27°C) and tolerant of a cool room; keep it above 50°F (10°C).
card.soil: An airy mix with bark and perlite. It climbs, and the roots want air as much as water.
card.feeding: Balanced feed at half strength every second or third watering in the growing season.
card.repotting: Every spring while it is growing fast. Give it something to climb.

common_problems.problem: Crispy edges and leaf drop
common_problems.fix: Dry air. This is the whole story with this plant. Get it above 60% humidity — a cabinet or terrarium is the honest answer.

common_problems.problem: Powdery white coating
common_problems.fix: Mildew from still, damp air. Improve the airflow; humidity without circulation is what causes it.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs.

card.summary: Grape ivy: glossy leaves in three parts on vines that climb by tendrils, like the grapevine it is related to. One of the most tolerant vines for a dim room and dry air, and the easiest member of its genus by a distance.
card.light: Bright indirect light, no direct sun. This is a jungle vine and the leaves mark easily.
card.water: Water when the top 2–3 cm is dry. It forgives a missed watering far better than the rex begonia vine does. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–80°F (15–27°C) and tolerant of a cool room; keep it above 50°F (10°C).
card.soil: An airy mix with bark and perlite. It climbs, and the roots want air as much as water.
card.feeding: Balanced feed at half strength every second or third watering in the growing season.
card.repotting: Every spring while it is growing fast. Give it something to climb.

common_problems.problem: Powdery white coating
common_problems.fix: Mildew from still, damp air. Improve the airflow; humidity without circulation is what causes it.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs.

card.summary: Creeping fig: small, heart-shaped leaves on thin stems that cling to whatever they touch with tiny roots, the way ivy does. Indoors it trails from a pot or climbs a moss pole — and on a wall it is hard to get off, so choose the surface.
card.light: Medium to bright indirect light. Unlike the tree figs it is an understorey climber, and it scorches in hard direct sun.
card.water: Keep the compost lightly damp. The leaves are thin and it crisps within days of drying out — and crisped leaves don't recover. As a starting point, water every 4 days.
card.humidity: Above 50%; the thin leaves crisp in dry air.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–80°F (15–27°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C). Drafts and sudden changes are what make figs drop leaves.
card.soil: A loam-based compost (John Innes No. 2 or its equivalent) with perlite mixed through. Ficus want weight and structure around the roots rather than the airy mixes aroids like.
card.feeding: Balanced feed at half strength every two to four weeks in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every spring while it is growing, or keep it in the same pot and trim it back.

common_problems.problem: Leaves crisp and brown all at once
common_problems.fix: It dried out. Water more often; creeping fig is far thirstier than the tree figs.

common_problems.problem: Leaves dropping after you moved it
common_problems.fix: Ficus dislike change — light, temperature, position, all of it. Put it somewhere bright and leave it there. Resist the urge to fix it; the drop stops within a few weeks.

common_problems.problem: Brown spots spreading from the leaf edges
common_problems.fix: Overwatering. The roots are suffocating. Let the top third dry out fully before the next water, and check the pot drains freely.

common_problems.problem: Bare lower stem, leaves only at the top
common_problems.fix: Not enough light. Move it into the brightest spot you have and prune the top back in spring — it branches from below the cut.

common_problems.problem: Sticky leaves and a black sooty film
common_problems.fix: Scale insects on the stems and leaf undersides. Scrape them off with a fingernail, then treat with horticultural soap every week for a month.

card.toxicity: Mildly toxic to cats and dogs. The milky sap irritates the mouth and stomach and can irritate skin on contact, so wear gloves when pruning.

card.summary: The Chinese money plant: round coin-shaped leaves on long stalks radiating from a central stem. It was carried out of Yunnan by a Norwegian missionary in 1946 and spread through Scandinavia entirely by cuttings passed between friends, decades before it reached the trade.
card.light: Bright indirect light, and turn the pot weekly — a pilea leans hard toward its light source and goes permanently lopsided otherwise.
card.water: Let the top half of the pot dry out, then water thoroughly. The leaves store water — a peperomia would much rather be dry. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine for most; the trailing kinds prefer above 60%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–80°F (15–27°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C).
card.soil: Peperomias have small, shallow root systems and semi-succulent leaves. A light, airy mix in a small pot is the whole secret; a big pot of wet compost is the whole problem.
card.feeding: A weak balanced feed monthly in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Rarely, and into a pot barely bigger than the last. Peperomias are happiest tight.

common_problems.problem: No babies
common_problems.fix: Too young, or not enough light. Give it a bright spot and wait — pileas pup freely once established.

common_problems.problem: Leaning heavily to one side
common_problems.fix: It grows toward light faster than most. Turn the pot a quarter turn every week.

common_problems.problem: Yellow lower leaves dropping
common_problems.fix: Overwatering, or simply age as the stem lengthens. Let it dry out more between waterings; a bare lower stem on an older pilea is normal.

common_problems.problem: Curling or cupping leaves
common_problems.fix: Usually too much light; sometimes too little water. Move it out of direct sun and check the compost.

card.toxicity: Not on the ASPCA's list itself, only its relatives, so we don't call it pet-safe. Keep it out of reach of a pet that chews.

card.summary: The aluminium plant: quilted dark-green leaves with raised silver patches that look painted on. A fast, bushy grower that turns leggy within a year or two, so pinch it back often and root the tips to keep the pot full.

card.summary: The prayer plant proper: velvety leaves patterned in herringbone red veins or dark chocolate blotches, which fold upright at night and open again at dawn. The movement is real and worth watching — it is driven by water pressure in a hinge at the base of each leaf.
card.light: Medium indirect light. Prayer plants grow on a forest floor and direct sun bleaches the pattern out of them within days. They are one of the few genuinely good plants for a north-facing room.
card.water: Keep evenly damp — never soggy, never dry — and use rainwater or filtered water if you can. Tap water is the most common cause of the brown edges this family is famous for. As a starting point, water every 5 days.
card.humidity: Above 60%. Below that, the edges brown and it will not stop.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 60°F (15°C). Cold drafts and sudden drops curl and brown the leaves.
card.soil: A light, moisture-retentive mix — compost with perlite and a little bark. The roots are fine and shallow, so a wide shallow pot beats a deep one.
card.feeding: A balanced feed at quarter to half strength monthly in spring and summer. They are sensitive to over-feeding.
card.repotting: Every spring, into a shallow pot. Divide the clump at the same time if it has spread.

common_problems.problem: Brown crispy edges on every leaf
common_problems.fix: Dry air, or minerals in tap water. Usually both. Get the humidity above 60% and switch to rainwater or filtered water. Existing damage will not heal.

common_problems.problem: Leaves curling inward
common_problems.fix: Thirsty, or the air is too dry. Water and raise the humidity; the leaves uncurl within a day if that was it.

common_problems.problem: Leaves staying folded up all day
common_problems.fix: Stress — too dry, too cold, or too dark. The folding is normal at night. All day means something is wrong: check water, warmth and light in that order.

common_problems.problem: Fine webbing under the leaves
common_problems.fix: Spider mites, which love this family. Shower the plant and treat weekly for a month; raise the humidity or they return.

common_problems.problem: Brown crispy edges on every leaf
common_problems.fix: Dry air, or minerals in tap water. Usually both. Get the humidity above 60% and switch to rainwater or filtered water. Existing damage will not heal.

common_problems.problem: Leaves curling inward
common_problems.fix: Thirsty, or the air is too dry. Water and raise the humidity; the leaves uncurl within a day if that was it.

common_problems.problem: Leaves staying folded up all day

common_problems.problem: Fine webbing under the leaves
common_problems.fix: Spider mites, which love this family. Shower the plant and treat weekly for a month; raise the humidity or they return.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs, which is much of their appeal.

card.summary: The Boston fern: arching fronds of fine leaflets, the Victorian parlour plant that never went away. It wants what no centrally-heated room offers — constant damp and humid air — which is why it is best kept in a bathroom, and why it sheds leaflets over the carpet everywhere else.
card.light: Medium indirect light, and never direct sun. A bright north window or a well-lit bathroom is close to ideal.
card.water: Keep the compost damp at all times — this is the one plant on this list where 'let it dry out' is wrong. Standing the pot in a shallow tray of water for an hour once a week suits it. As a starting point, water every 4 days.
card.humidity: Above 60%. A fern in dry air is a fern on its way out.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–75°F (15–24°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C). Hot, dry air near a heater does more harm than cool.
card.soil: A mix that holds water without turning to mud: compost with perlite and a little bark. Ferns have fine roots that must never dry out completely.
card.feeding: A weak balanced feed monthly in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every spring. Divide the clump at the same time if it has filled the pot.

common_problems.problem: Fronds going brown and crisp from the tips
common_problems.fix: Dry air, or the compost dried out. Raise the humidity and never let the pot go fully dry. A bathroom is the easy answer.

common_problems.problem: Leaflets dropping all over the floor
common_problems.fix: Dry heat, usually from a radiator. Move it away from the heat source and raise the humidity.

common_problems.problem: Yellowing fronds in a wet pot
common_problems.fix: It is sitting in water rather than damp compost. Damp, not waterlogged — make sure the pot drains and the saucer empties.

common_problems.problem: Brown dots in rows under the fronds
common_problems.fix: Spores. Completely normal. Nothing to do; it means the fern is mature and happy.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs.

card.summary: The staghorn fern: two kinds of frond — flat round shield fronds that clasp the mount and brown as they age, and forked antler fronds that hang out from it. It is an epiphyte and is happiest mounted on a board with sphagnum rather than in a pot of compost.
card.light: Medium indirect light, and never direct sun. A bright north window or a well-lit bathroom is close to ideal.
card.water: Soak the whole mount or root ball in water for ten minutes, then let it drain and dry out somewhat before the next soak — usually weekly. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Above 60%. A fern in dry air is a fern on its way out.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–80°F (15–27°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C).
card.soil: Staghorns are epiphytes that grow on tree trunks. Mounted on a board with sphagnum behind them is how they are happiest; in a pot, use pure bark and moss rather than compost.
card.feeding: A weak balanced feed monthly in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every spring. Divide the clump at the same time if it has filled the pot.

common_problems.problem: The flat round shield frond turning brown
common_problems.fix: Normal. Shield fronds brown and stay on as the plant's anchor. Leave it exactly where it is — removing it damages the plant.

common_problems.problem: Black spots spreading on the antler fronds
common_problems.fix: Too wet, or water sitting on the fronds in still air. Water at the base, improve airflow, and let it dry between soaks.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs.

card.summary: Rabbit's foot fern: lacy fronds and thick furry rhizomes that crawl over the edge of the pot and hang down like paws. The rhizomes are the point and must stay on the surface — a rabbit's foot fern potted 'properly', with them buried, will die.
card.light: Medium indirect light, and never direct sun. A bright north window or a well-lit bathroom is close to ideal.
card.water: Keep damp, and leave the furry rhizomes sitting on top of the compost where they belong — burying them kills the plant. As a starting point, water every 5 days.
card.humidity: Above 60%. A fern in dry air is a fern on its way out.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–75°F (15–24°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C).
card.soil: A mix that holds water without turning to mud: compost with perlite and a little bark. Ferns have fine roots that must never dry out completely.
card.feeding: A weak balanced feed monthly in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every spring. Divide the clump at the same time if it has filled the pot.

card.summary: The button fern: low, arching fronds of small, round, dark-green leaflets like buttons on a string. It comes from New Zealand and, unusually for a fern, wants to dry slightly between waterings — it rots if kept wet.
card.light: Medium indirect light, and never direct sun. A bright north window or a well-lit bathroom is close to ideal.
card.water: Let the top of the compost dry slightly between waterings. Unusually for a fern, button fern rots if it is kept constantly wet. As a starting point, water every 6 days.
card.humidity: Moderate; it copes with drier air than most ferns.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–75°F (15–24°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C).

card.repotting: Every spring. Divide the clump at the same time if it has filled the pot.

common_problems.problem: Fronds yellowing and the crown going soft
common_problems.fix: Kept too wet. Let the top of the compost dry between waterings, in a shallow pot that drains well.

common_problems.problem: Crisp, brown fronds
common_problems.fix: It dried right out, or sits in hot sun. Water before it dries completely, and keep it out of direct sun.

common_problems.problem: Brown dots in rows under the leaflets
common_problems.fix: Spores. Completely normal. Nothing to do.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs.

card.summary: The polka dot begonia: angel-wing leaves, olive above with silver spots, deep red beneath, on tall cane stems, with clusters of white flowers. It is the begonia that Instagram made ubiquitous, and it wants humid air that is nonetheless moving — still damp air gives it mildew.
card.light: Bright indirect light. Begonias want brightness without a ray of direct sun landing on the leaves, which mark permanently.
card.water: Water when the top of the compost is dry, around the edge of the pot rather than over the leaves. Water sitting on a begonia leaf overnight is how mildew starts. As a starting point, water every 6 days.
card.humidity: Above 60%, but with air moving — still humid air gives them mildew.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–75°F (18–24°C); keep it above 60°F (15°C) and out of drafts.
card.soil: A light open mix. Begonia roots are fine and shallow and rot readily; many growers use a shallow pot and an aroid-style mix.
card.feeding: A balanced feed at half strength every two to four weeks in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every spring, into a shallow wide pot. Cane begonias get top-heavy and want staking.

common_problems.problem: White powdery patches on the leaves
common_problems.fix: Powdery mildew — humid air with no movement. Improve airflow, stop watering over the leaves, remove affected leaves, and treat if it spreads.

common_problems.problem: Leaves dropping suddenly
common_problems.fix: A cold draught or a dry spell. Keep it above 15 °C and evenly damp.

common_problems.problem: Leggy stems with leaves only at the top
common_problems.fix: Not enough light. Move it brighter and cut back hard in spring — cane begonias respond well.

common_problems.problem: Brown crisp edges
common_problems.fix: Dry air. Raise humidity, keeping the air moving.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs — the tubers most of all. Causes mouth irritation and vomiting.

card.summary: Angel wing begonias: cane begonias with long, wing-shaped leaves, usually spotted with silver, on bamboo-like stems, and hanging clusters of pink, red or white flowers. Easy, in flower for months, and leggy — pinch and prune to keep them bushy.

card.summary: The African violet: a rosette of furry leaves and clusters of small velvety flowers, on a plant that can bloom almost year-round on an east windowsill.
card.light: Bright indirect light — an east window is close to perfect. African violets flower reliably at a light level that suits an ordinary room, which is much of why they have been popular for a century.
card.water: Water from below: stand the pot in 2 cm of tepid water for twenty minutes, then drain. Cold water on the leaves leaves permanent pale rings. As a starting point, water every 6 days.
card.humidity: Above 50%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 60°F (15°C), and off a cold windowsill at night.
card.soil: A light open mix in a small shallow pot. African violets flower best when snug and rot if the crown sits in wet compost.
card.feeding: A high-phosphorus African violet feed at quarter strength with most waterings while in flower.
card.repotting: Once a year, into the same size pot with fresh mix. Bury the bare stem a little deeper each time.

common_problems.problem: Pale rings and blotches on the leaves
common_problems.fix: Cold water splashed on the leaves. Water from below with tepid water. The marks are permanent on those leaves.

common_problems.problem: No flowers
common_problems.fix: Too little light, too big a pot, or too much nitrogen. Move it to a bright east window, keep it snug, and use a high-phosphorus feed.

common_problems.problem: Crown going soft and brown
common_problems.fix: Water sat in the centre of the rosette. Water from below only. A rotted crown is usually fatal — take leaf cuttings while you can.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs.

card.summary: The lipstick plant: trailing stems of glossy, dark leaves ending in clusters of red, tubular flowers that push out of dark calyces like lipstick from its tube. A gesneriad, related to African violets, that grows on trees in the wild.
card.light: Bright indirect light — an east window is close to perfect. African violets flower reliably at a light level that suits an ordinary room, which is much of why they have been popular for a century.
card.water: Let the top few centimetres dry, then water thoroughly. It is an epiphyte and hates soggy roots. As a starting point, water every 6 days.
card.humidity: Above 50%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 60°F (15°C) and out of cold drafts.
card.soil: Compost lightened with orchid bark and perlite. In the wild it grows on trees, and its roots want air.
card.feeding: A high-phosphorus African violet feed at quarter strength with most waterings while in flower.
card.repotting: Every two or three years; it flowers best a little potbound.

common_problems.problem: No flowers
common_problems.fix: Too little light, or a pot that is too big. Move it brighter and keep it snug in its pot; it flowers on new growth in spring and summer.

common_problems.problem: Leaves dropping
common_problems.fix: Cold, a draught, or a sudden dry spell. Keep it above 15 °C, away from cold glass, and water more steadily.

common_problems.problem: Long bare stems
common_problems.fix: Normal with age. Cut the stems back by a third after flowering; it branches from below the cut.

card.summary: The Mexican snowball: a tight rosette of pale blue-green leaves coated in a chalky bloom that protects it from sun — and which rubs off permanently on a fingerprint. It needs four to six hours of direct sun to stay compact; anything less and it stretches into a pale tower that cannot be fixed.
card.light: As much direct sun as you can give it — four to six hours minimum. An echeveria in a normal room stretches into a pale tower within weeks, and no amount of later light will make it compact again.
card.water: Water thoroughly, then leave it until the pot is bone dry and the lower leaves have gone slightly soft. Never water into the rosette — water sitting in the centre rots it. As a starting point, water every 2 weeks.
card.humidity: Indifferent; dry air is ideal.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C) while growing; a cool, dry winter around 50–55°F (10–13°C) suits it. Keep it frost-free, above 40°F (4°C).
card.soil: Cactus compost cut with more grit. A terracotta pot helps because it wicks water out of the mix and away from the roots.
card.feeding: A weak cactus feed two or three times over the summer.
card.repotting: Every two or three years in spring, into a pot barely larger than the rosette.

common_problems.problem: Stretched, pale, spaced-out leaves
common_problems.fix: Not enough light. This is not reversible. Cut the head off, let it callus for a few days, and re-root it in full sun. The stump usually produces offsets.

common_problems.problem: Mushy translucent lower leaves
common_problems.fix: Overwatering. Stop watering. Remove the affected leaves and let it dry out completely.

common_problems.problem: Shrivelled wrinkled leaves
common_problems.fix: Genuinely thirsty. Water thoroughly and it plumps back up within a day or two.

common_problems.problem: White cottony blobs between the leaves
common_problems.fix: Mealybugs. Alcohol on a cotton bud, every few days for a month — they hide deep in the rosette.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs.

common_problems.problem: Stretched, pale, spaced-out leaves
common_problems.fix: Not enough light. This is not reversible. Cut the head off, let it callus for a few days, and re-root it in full sun. The stump usually produces offsets.

common_problems.problem: Mushy translucent lower leaves
common_problems.fix: Overwatering. Stop watering. Remove the affected leaves and let it dry out completely.

common_problems.problem: Shrivelled wrinkled leaves
common_problems.fix: Genuinely thirsty. Water thoroughly and it plumps back up within a day or two.

common_problems.problem: White cottony blobs between the leaves
common_problems.fix: Mealybugs. Alcohol on a cotton bud, every few days for a month — they hide deep in the rosette.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs.

card.summary: String of buttons: pairs of triangular, grey-green leaves stacked along upright stems as if threaded on a string, edged in red in strong light. Easy and slow-growing.
card.light: Four to six hours of direct sun. A jade in a dim room stretches into a thin pale thing that never regains its compact shape.
card.water: Water thoroughly, then not again until the pot is bone dry and the leaves have lost a little of their firmness. In winter, once a month is plenty. As a starting point, water every 2 weeks.
card.humidity: Indifferent; dry air is fine.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C). A cool winter around 50–55°F (10–13°C) helps it flower; keep it above 40°F (4°C) and frost-free.

card.feeding: A weak cactus feed two or three times over the summer.
card.repotting: Every three or four years, and into a heavy pot — a mature jade is top-heavy and a plastic pot will tip.

common_problems.problem: Leaves dropping at a touch
common_problems.fix: Overwatering, almost always. Stop watering until the pot is fully dry, then water far less often.

common_problems.problem: Stretched pale stems with leaves far apart
common_problems.fix: Not enough light. Move it into direct sun and cut the stretched growth back — the cuttings will root.

common_problems.problem: Red edges on the leaves
common_problems.fix: Sun and cool nights. This is a good sign, not a problem. Nothing to fix; it is the plant colouring up.

common_problems.problem: White cottony spots in the leaf joints
common_problems.fix: Mealybugs. Dab each one with alcohol on a cotton bud and check again weekly for a month.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs; causes vomiting and lethargy. Not a hazard to people.

card.summary: The tree aeonium: glossy rosettes of leaves on the ends of bare, branching stems, often sold in the near-black form 'Zwartkop'. It grows in the cool months and rests in summer, when the rosettes close up tight.
card.light: Bright light, with direct sun from autumn to spring. Aeoniums grow in winter and rest in the summer heat, when the rosettes close up and drop leaves — that is normal, not dying.
card.water: Water when the top half of the pot is dry while it is growing, from autumn to spring. During its summer rest, water lightly and only now and then. As a starting point, water every 10 days.
card.humidity: Indifferent; dry air is ideal.
card.temperature: Prefers it mild: 50–75°F (10–24°C). Summer heat sends it into its rest; keep it above 40°F (4°C).

It can be made to rebloom, but only with fourteen hours of complete darkness a night for six weeks — which is why it never happens by accident.

common_problems.problem: Flowers once, then never again
common_problems.fix: Kalanchoes are short-day plants and need long nights to set buds. Give it fourteen hours of total darkness a night for six weeks in autumn.

common_problems.problem: Stretched leggy growth
common_problems.fix: Not enough light. Move it into direct sun, and cut it back in spring.

common_problems.problem: Mushy stem at the base
common_problems.fix: Overwatering. Take healthy cuttings and start again.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs. Kalanchoes contain cardiac glycosides, which affect the heart — this is one of the more seriously toxic houseplants sold, and worth keeping out of reach.

card.summary: Houseleeks, or hens and chicks: flat rosettes that multiply into mats of offsets, hardy to well below freezing. They were planted on roofs across Europe for centuries in the belief they turned away lightning.
card.light: Full sun. Houseleeks are alpine plants, hardy to well below freezing, and they do better on a windowsill that gets cold at night — or outdoors — than in a warm room.
card.water: Water thoroughly, then leave it until the pot is bone dry and the lower leaves have gone slightly soft. Never water into the rosette — water sitting in the centre rots it. As a starting point, water every 2 weeks.
card.humidity: Indifferent; dry air is ideal.
card.temperature: Frost-hardy — an outdoor plant at heart that does best with a cold winter. Indoors, give it the coolest bright spot you have.
card.soil: Cactus compost cut with more grit. A terracotta pot helps because it wicks water out of the mix and away from the roots.
card.feeding: A weak cactus feed two or three times over the summer.
card.repotting: Every two or three years in spring, into a pot barely larger than the rosette.

common_problems.problem: Stretched, pale, spaced-out leaves
common_problems.fix: Not enough light. This is not reversible. Cut the head off, let it callus for a few days, and re-root it in full sun. The stump usually produces offsets.

common_problems.problem: Mushy translucent lower leaves
common_problems.fix: Overwatering. Stop watering. Remove the affected leaves and let it dry out completely.

common_problems.problem: Shrivelled wrinkled leaves
common_problems.fix: Genuinely thirsty. Water thoroughly and it plumps back up within a day or two.

common_problems.problem: White cottony blobs between the leaves
common_problems.fix: Mealybugs. Alcohol on a cotton bud, every few days for a month — they hide deep in the rosette.

card.toxicity: Not on the ASPCA's list of toxic or non-toxic plants, so we don't call it pet-safe: not being listed is not the same as being tested. Keep it out of reach of a pet that chews.

card.summary: Burro's tail: long trailing stems packed with plump blue-green leaves that fall off at the slightest touch — which is both its main fault and its easiest method of propagation. Hang it somewhere nothing brushes past.
card.light: As much direct sun as you can give it — four to six hours minimum. An echeveria in a normal room stretches into a pale tower within weeks, and no amount of later light will make it compact again.
card.water: Water thoroughly, then leave it until the pot is bone dry and the lower leaves have gone slightly soft. Never water into the rosette — water sitting in the centre rots it. As a starting point, water every 2 weeks.
card.humidity: Indifferent; dry air is ideal.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–80°F (15–27°C); fine cooler in winter, but keep it frost-free, above 40°F (4°C).
card.soil: Cactus compost cut with more grit. A terracotta pot helps because it wicks water out of the mix and away from the roots.

card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C). Cold, wet soil is what rots it.

card.summary: Crown of thorns: woody, viciously spiny stems with fresh green leaves at the tips and small red, pink or yellow bracts that it carries for much of the year. It takes more water than a cactus, and drops its leaves when it is too dry or too cold — then grows them back.

card.water: Water when the top half of the pot is dry. It is a leafy shrub, not a cactus, and drops leaves if left dry too long; water less in winter. As a starting point, water every 10 days.

card.summary: The Christmas or Thanksgiving cactus: flat segmented stems that arch over and, in late autumn, hang tubular flowers off every tip. It is a forest cactus that grows in tree forks in Brazil, not a desert plant — so it wants more water and less sun than its shape suggests.
card.light: Bright indirect light. Holiday cacti are forest cacti that grow in tree forks, not desert plants — direct sun reddens and scorches the segments.
card.water: Water when the top half of the pot is dry — more often than a desert cactus, less than a houseplant. Keep it drier for six weeks in autumn to set buds. As a starting point, water every 10 days.
card.humidity: Above 50%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–75°F (15–24°C). Cool autumn nights around 50–60°F (10–15°C) help it set buds; keep it above 45°F (7°C).
card.soil: More like an orchid mix than a desert cactus one: open, bark-heavy, free-draining, but not pure grit.
card.feeding: A balanced feed at half strength monthly from spring to late summer, then stop.
card.repotting: Every three or four years, after flowering. They bloom better potbound.

common_problems.problem: Buds dropping before they open
common_problems.fix: It was moved, or the temperature or watering changed. Once the buds form, leave it alone — do not turn it, move it, or change the routine.

common_problems.problem: No flowers
common_problems.fix: It needs cool nights and long darkness in autumn to set buds. From early autumn, give it twelve to fourteen hours of darkness and nights around 12–15 °C for six weeks.

common_problems.problem: Limp wrinkled segments
common_problems.fix: Either too dry or rotting roots. Check the roots before watering.

common_problems.problem: Red or purple segments
common_problems.fix: Too much direct sun, or hungry. Move it out of direct sun and feed in spring.

card.toxicity: Not on the ASPCA's list itself, only its relatives, so we don't call it pet-safe. Keep it out of reach of a pet that chews.

card.summary: Bunny ears cactus: flat oval pads sprouting in pairs, dotted with tufts of fine golden glochids. It has no long spines, which makes it look harmless — it isn't.
card.light: Full direct sun, as much as there is. Desert cacti etiolate into pale asparagus in anything less.
card.water: Water thoroughly in summer once the pot is completely dry, roughly every three weeks. From late autumn to early spring, stop almost entirely — a cold wet cactus is a dead cactus. As a starting point, water every 3 weeks.
card.humidity: Indifferent; dry air is ideal.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–90°F (18–32°C) while growing; a cool, dry winter at 40–50°F (4–10°C) is fine. Keep it frost-free.
card.soil: Cactus compost with at least half grit or pumice, in a terracotta pot. Drainage is the entire discipline with cacti.
card.feeding: A weak cactus feed two or three times over the summer.
card.repotting: Every three or four years. Use folded newspaper or thick gloves as a handle.

common_problems.problem: Soft brown patches at the base
common_problems.fix: Rot from water in cold conditions. Cut above the rot, callus the cut, and re-root. Keep it dry all winter.

common_problems.problem: Pale stretched narrow growth at the top
common_problems.fix: Not enough light. Move it into full sun. The stretched part stays stretched.

common_problems.problem: Corky brown patches low down
common_problems.fix: Normal ageing on an older cactus. Nothing to fix.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs, but the glochids — the fine hair-like spines — embed in skin and are miserable to remove. Handle with care.

card.soil: More like an orchid mix than a desert cactus one: open, bark-heavy, free-draining, but not pure grit.
card.feeding: A balanced feed at half strength monthly from spring to late summer, then stop.
card.repotting: Every three or four years, after flowering. They bloom better potbound.

common_problems.problem: Buds dropping before they open
common_problems.fix: It was moved, or the temperature or watering changed. Once the buds form, leave it alone — do not turn it, move it, or change the routine.

common_problems.problem: No flowers
common_problems.fix: It needs cool nights and long darkness in autumn to set buds. From early autumn, give it twelve to fourteen hours of darkness and nights around 12–15 °C for six weeks.

common_problems.problem: Limp wrinkled segments
common_problems.fix: Either too dry or rotting roots. Check the roots before watering.

common_problems.problem: Red or purple segments
common_problems.fix: Too much direct sun, or hungry. Move it out of direct sun and feed in spring.

card.toxicity: Not on the ASPCA's list itself, only its relatives, so we don't call it pet-safe. Keep it out of reach of a pet that chews.

card.summary: Living stones: a pair of fused leaves flush with the ground, patterned to look like the pebbles around them. Each year the plant absorbs the old pair of leaves to grow a new one, and watering during that changeover is the standard way people kill them.
card.light: Full sun, four to six hours of it. In the wild only the flat translucent window on top of each leaf shows above the gravel, and the plant lives on the light that comes through it — give it less and it stretches upward into a soft pale column that never recovers its shape.
card.water: Far less often than the reminder suggests, and only at the right point in the year. Lithops follow a strict cycle: water lightly in autumn and again in spring, and give them nothing at all through winter while a new pair of leaves is absorbing the old pair. Watering during that changeover is the standard way people kill them. As a starting point, water monthly.
card.humidity: Indifferent; dry air is ideal.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); fine down to 40°F (4°C) if kept dry, but never frost.
card.soil: Cactus compost with at least half grit or pumice, in a terracotta pot. Drainage is the entire discipline with cacti.
card.feeding: A weak cactus feed two or three times over the summer.
card.repotting: Every four or five years at most, into a deep narrow pot — the taproot is long.

common_problems.problem: Split, burst or mushy body
common_problems.fix: Watered during the dormant period or during the leaf change. Stop watering completely until the old leaves are dry papery shells.

common_problems.problem: Stretching upward into a column
common_problems.fix: Not enough light. Move it into full sun; this does not reverse.

common_problems.problem: Old leaves not drying up
common_problems.fix: Watered too early in the cycle. Withhold water entirely and let the new pair draw the old one down.

card.toxicity: Not on the ASPCA's list itself, only its relatives, so we don't call it pet-safe. Keep it out of reach of a pet that chews.

card.summary: The moth orchid: arching sprays of flat flowers that last for months, on a plant with no bulbs and only a few thick leaves. It is an epiphyte whose silvery-green aerial roots photosynthesise, which is why it is sold in a clear pot and why it must never be planted in compost.
card.light: Bright indirect light — an east window, or a metre back from a south one. A moth orchid's leaves should be a mid grass-green; dark forest-green leaves mean too little light, which is the usual reason one never reflowers.
card.water: Soak the bark thoroughly under the tap once a week, let it drain completely, and never leave water in the pot cover. Silvery-white roots mean thirsty; green roots mean it has had enough. As a starting point, water every 8 days.
card.humidity: Above 50%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 60°F (15°C). Nights about 10°F (5–6°C) cooler for a few weeks in autumn help it rebloom.
card.soil: Never compost. Phalaenopsis roots are photosynthetic and need air: coarse bark, or sphagnum if you water carefully, in a pot with drainage. The clear pots they are sold in are useful — you can see the roots.
card.feeding: A weak orchid feed with every second watering while in growth.
card.repotting: Every two years, into fresh bark, after flowering. Old bark breaks down into something that holds water and kills the roots.

common_problems.problem: Never reflowers
common_problems.fix: Not enough light, or no temperature drop. Give it a brighter spot, and a few weeks of nights around 16 °C in autumn — that drop is what triggers a new spike.

common_problems.problem: Limp wrinkled leaves
common_problems.fix: Root loss, usually from sitting wet, so the plant cannot drink. Unpot it and look: brown hollow roots are dead. Cut them off, repot in fresh bark, keep humidity up while it rebuilds.

common_problems.problem: Yellowing lowest leaf
common_problems.fix: Normal — orchids shed the oldest leaf. Nothing to do unless several go at once.

common_problems.problem: The flower spike turning brown after flowering
common_problems.fix: Finished. Cut it off at the base. A green spike can instead be cut just above a node and may branch into a second flush.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs.

card.summary: An orchid that flowers along the length of its leafless canes rather than on a spike, covering them in scented blooms. It needs a genuinely cold, dry winter rest — nights near 10 °C and almost no water for six weeks — to set buds, which is why the ones sold in flower rarely repeat indoors.
card.light: Bright indirect light — an east window, or a metre back from a south one. A moth orchid's leaves should be a mid grass-green; dark forest-green leaves mean too little light, which is the usual reason one never reflowers.
card.water: Water thoroughly while in growth, then keep it much drier and cooler through winter — that rest is what makes it flower. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Above 50%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–80°F (15–27°C). Nobile types need cool autumn nights around 50–55°F (10–13°C) to set flowers.
card.soil: Never compost. Phalaenopsis roots are photosynthetic and need air: coarse bark, or sphagnum if you water carefully, in a pot with drainage. The clear pots they are sold in are useful — you can see the roots.
card.feeding: A weak orchid feed with every second watering while in growth.
card.repotting: Every two years, into fresh bark, after flowering. Old bark breaks down into something that holds water and kills the roots.

common_problems.problem: Never reflowers
common_problems.fix: Not enough light, or no temperature drop. Give it a brighter spot, and a few weeks of nights around 16 °C in autumn — that drop is what triggers a new spike.

common_problems.problem: Limp wrinkled leaves
common_problems.fix: Root loss, usually from sitting wet, so the plant cannot drink. Unpot it and look: brown hollow roots are dead. Cut them off, repot in fresh bark, keep humidity up while it rebuilds.

common_problems.problem: Yellowing lowest leaf
common_problems.fix: Normal — orchids shed the oldest leaf. Nothing to do unless several go at once.

common_problems.problem: The flower spike turning brown after flowering
common_problems.fix: Finished. Cut it off at the base. A green spike can instead be cut just above a node and may branch into a second flush.

card.toxicity: Not on the ASPCA's list itself, only its relatives, so we don't call it pet-safe. Keep it out of reach of a pet that chews.

card.summary: The corsage orchid: large, heavily scented flowers with an extravagant frilled lip, from thick pseudobulbs. It wants brighter light than a moth orchid — some direct sun — and a proper dry period between waterings, which its pseudobulbs are built to carry it through.
card.light: Bright indirect light — an east window, or a metre back from a south one. A moth orchid's leaves should be a mid grass-green; dark forest-green leaves mean too little light, which is the usual reason one never reflowers.
card.water: Let the bark dry out almost completely between waterings; the pseudobulbs carry the plant through. As a starting point, water every 8 days.
card.humidity: Above 50%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C) by day with nights around 55–65°F (13–18°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C).
card.soil: Never compost. Phalaenopsis roots are photosynthetic and need air: coarse bark, or sphagnum if you water carefully, in a pot with drainage. The clear pots they are sold in are useful — you can see the roots.
card.feeding: A weak orchid feed with every second watering while in growth.
card.repotting: Every two years, into fresh bark, after flowering. Old bark breaks down into something that holds water and kills the roots.

common_problems.fix: Not enough light, or no temperature drop. Give it a brighter spot, and a few weeks of nights around 16 °C in autumn — that drop is what triggers a new spike.

common_problems.fix: Root loss, usually from sitting wet, so the plant cannot drink. Unpot it and look: brown hollow roots are dead. Cut them off, repot in fresh bark, keep humidity up while it rebuilds.

common_problems.problem: Yellowing lowest leaf
common_problems.fix: Normal — orchids shed the oldest leaf. Nothing to do unless several go at once.

common_problems.problem: The flower spike turning brown after flowering
common_problems.fix: Finished. Cut it off at the base. A green spike can instead be cut just above a node and may branch into a second flush.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs.

card.summary: The chocolate orchid: a hybrid that sends up long, branching sprays of small red-brown and white flowers that smell of chocolate or vanilla. Easier than it looks, and it flowers from each new pseudobulb.
card.light: Bright indirect light — an east window, or a metre back from a south one. A moth orchid's leaves should be a mid grass-green; dark forest-green leaves mean too little light, which is the usual reason one never reflowers.
card.water: Water thoroughly when the bark is nearly dry, and more often while new growths are developing; the pseudobulbs should stay plump. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Above 50%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C) by day with nights about 10°F (5°C) cooler; keep it above 55°F (13°C).
card.soil: Never compost. Phalaenopsis roots are photosynthetic and need air: coarse bark, or sphagnum if you water carefully, in a pot with drainage. The clear pots they are sold in are useful — you can see the roots.
card.feeding: A weak orchid feed with every second watering while in growth.
card.repotting: Every two years, into fresh bark, after flowering. Old bark breaks down into something that holds water and kills the roots.

common_problems.problem: Never reflowers
common_problems.fix: Not enough light, or no temperature drop. Give it a brighter spot, and a few weeks of nights around 16 °C in autumn — that drop is what triggers a new spike.

common_problems.problem: Limp wrinkled leaves
common_problems.fix: Root loss, usually from sitting wet, so the plant cannot drink. Unpot it and look: brown hollow roots are dead. Cut them off, repot in fresh bark, keep humidity up while it rebuilds.

common_problems.problem: Yellowing lowest leaf
common_problems.fix: Normal — orchids shed the oldest leaf. Nothing to do unless several go at once.

common_problems.problem: The flower spike turning brown after flowering
common_problems.fix: Finished. Cut it off at the base. A green spike can instead be cut just above a node and may branch into a second flush.

card.toxicity: Not on the ASPCA's list itself, only its relatives, so we don't call it pet-safe. Keep it out of reach of a pet that chews.

card.summary: Maudiae-type slipper orchids: mottled green leaves and a single waxy flower with a pouch-shaped lip, in green and white or deep red-purple, lasting for weeks. Slipper orchids want less light than a moth orchid and should never dry out completely.
card.light: Bright indirect light — an east window, or a metre back from a south one. A moth orchid's leaves should be a mid grass-green; dark forest-green leaves mean too little light, which is the usual reason one never reflowers.
card.water: Keep the mix lightly moist. Slipper orchids have no pseudobulbs to store water, so they shouldn't dry out completely. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Above 50%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C).
card.soil: Never compost. Phalaenopsis roots are photosynthetic and need air: coarse bark, or sphagnum if you water carefully, in a pot with drainage. The clear pots they are sold in are useful — you can see the roots.
card.feeding: A weak orchid feed with every second watering while in growth.
card.repotting: Every two years, into fresh bark, after flowering. Old bark breaks down into something that holds water and kills the roots.

common_problems.problem: No new flowers
common_problems.fix: Too little light, or no new growth to flower from — each growth flowers once. Give it bright indirect light; a plant that is growing well will flower.

common_problems.problem: Rot in the centre of a growth
common_problems.fix: Water left sitting in the crown. Water the mix, not the leaves, and tip out any water that collects in the fan.

common_problems.problem: Brown leaf tips
common_problems.fix: Salts from fertiliser or hard water. Flush the pot through with rainwater monthly, and feed weakly.

card.toxicity: Not on the ASPCA's list of toxic or non-toxic plants, so we don't call it pet-safe: not being listed is not the same as being tested. Keep it out of reach of a pet that chews.

card.summary: The gardenia: glossy dark leaves and thick white flowers with one of the strongest scents of any plant. It is also the most demanding plant on this list — it needs acid soil, rainwater, humidity above 60% and absolute consistency, and it drops every bud if any of those slip.
card.light: Bright light with a few hours of direct sun. Gardenias are demanding plants and light is the least of it.
card.water: Keep evenly damp with rainwater or filtered water. Hard tap water will yellow the leaves within a couple of months whatever else you do. As a starting point, water every 5 days.
card.humidity: Above 60%, consistently.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–75°F (18–24°C) by day and a little cooler at night. Sudden swings and drafts make it drop its buds.
card.soil: Gardenias need acid soil, pH 5 to 6. In ordinary compost or with hard tap water they cannot take up iron and go yellow between the veins. Use ericaceous compost and rainwater.
card.feeding: An ericaceous or acid-loving plant feed every two weeks in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every second spring, into fresh ericaceous compost.

common_problems.problem: Yellow leaves with green veins
common_problems.fix: Iron deficiency from soil or water that is too alkaline — the classic gardenia problem. Repot into ericaceous compost, water with rainwater, and feed with a sequestered iron product.

common_problems.problem: Buds dropping before opening
common_problems.fix: A change in temperature, light, watering or humidity. Gardenias object to all of them. Keep everything constant once buds form, and humidity above 60%.

common_problems.problem: Sticky leaves, black sooty mould
common_problems.fix: Scale or mealybugs. Treat weekly for a month and wipe the mould off.

card.toxicity: Mildly toxic to cats and dogs; causes vomiting and diarrhoea.

card.summary: Pink jasmine: a vigorous twining climber that covers itself in pink buds opening to white, scenting a whole room. It is sold trained around a hoop in midwinter and needs a cool, dry autumn to flower again — which is why most are treated as a one-season plant.
card.light: Bright light with direct sun. Indoors it needs the sunniest window there is; outdoors in summer it is happier still.
card.water: Keep damp in spring and summer, drier in autumn and winter. The cool dry autumn rest is what sets the buds. As a starting point, water every 5 days.
card.humidity: Above 50%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–75°F (15–24°C). Pink jasmine needs a cool spell — around 40–50°F (4–10°C) for several weeks in winter — to flower.
card.soil: A loam-based compost with grit for drainage. Jasmine is a vigorous climber and wants something with body to it.
card.feeding: A high-potash feed every two weeks from spring until flowering finishes.
card.repotting: Every second spring. Prune hard right after flowering — it flowers on the previous season's growth, so pruning later costs you next year's blooms.

common_problems.problem: No flowers
common_problems.fix: Too warm in autumn, or pruned at the wrong time. Give it six weeks of nights around 10 °C in autumn, and prune only immediately after flowering.

common_problems.problem: Yellow leaves dropping
common_problems.fix: Overwatering, or a pot that is too small. Check the drainage and repot in spring.

common_problems.problem: Red spider mite in a warm room
common_problems.fix: Dry heat. Raise humidity and treat weekly.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs.

card.summary: Chinese hibiscus: enormous flowers, each lasting a day or two, produced all summer on new growth if it gets enough sun and enough feeding. It is greedy on both counts and will not flower indoors without a genuinely sunny window.
card.light: As much direct sun as possible — six hours if you can. Hibiscus flower on new growth in strong light and simply do not bloom without it.
card.water: Keep damp through the growing season — daily in a hot room is normal — and much drier in winter. As a starting point, water every 4 days.
card.humidity: Above 50%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–85°F (15–29°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C). Cold makes it drop buds and leaves.
card.soil: A rich loam-based compost with grit. They are hungry and thirsty and still want the pot to drain.
card.feeding: A high-potash feed weekly through spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every spring while young. Prune in early spring to shape — flowers come on new wood.

common_problems.problem: Buds dropping before they open
common_problems.fix: Irregular watering, a move, or a sudden temperature change. Water on a steady routine and keep it in one place.

common_problems.problem: Yellow leaves
common_problems.fix: Overwatering, cold, or hunger. Check the drainage first, then feed — hibiscus are greedy.

common_problems.problem: No flowers
common_problems.fix: Not enough light or not enough potash. Move it into full sun and switch to a high-potash feed.

card.toxicity: Not on the ASPCA's list itself, only its relatives, so we don't call it pet-safe. Keep it out of reach of a pet that chews.

card.summary: The flamingo lily: smaller and narrower-leaved than the common anthurium, with a curled orange spadix like a pig's tail over a bright spathe. It is a little more tolerant of ordinary room conditions than the velvet anthuriums and flowers more freely.
card.light: Bright indirect light. The flowering kinds need it to keep producing spathes; the velvet-leaved ones scorch easily and want the same brightness filtered through a sheer curtain.
card.water: Water when the top of the mix is dry to the touch, and let it drain completely. In a bark mix that is often twice a week; in soil it would be a death sentence. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: 60% and up. This is the genus where humidity actually decides the outcome.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C); keep it above 60°F (15°C) and away from drafts and heaters.
card.soil: Anthuriums are epiphytes. The mix should look wrong: mostly orchid bark and perlite with a little coir, loose enough that water pours straight through. Standard compost suffocates them within a season.
card.feeding: A weak orchid feed every second watering while growing.
card.repotting: Every year or two, into a pot barely larger than the root ball. Bury the stem slightly deeper each time — anthuriums creep upward and go bald at the base otherwise.

common_problems.problem: Brown crispy leaf edges
common_problems.fix: Air too dry, or tap water minerals building up. Raise humidity above 60% and water with rain or filtered water if your tap is hard.

common_problems.problem: No flowers for months
common_problems.fix: Not enough light, or not enough phosphorus. Move it brighter and switch to a feed with a higher middle number through spring and summer.

common_problems.problem: Yellowing leaves with a soft brown base
common_problems.fix: Rot, almost always from a mix that holds water. Repot into bark and perlite, cutting away any root that is brown and mushy.

common_problems.problem: A bald woody stem with leaves only at the top
common_problems.fix: Normal upward creep. Repot deeper, or cut the top off below a set of aerial roots and re-root it.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and people if chewed — the sap carries insoluble calcium oxalate crystals, which burn the mouth and throat. Keep it off the floor if anything in the house tastes its way through life.

card.summary: Cyclamen: swept-back flowers in white, pink and red over marbled heart-shaped leaves, flowering right through winter. It wants a cool room — 12–15 °C — and collapses in a warm one, which is why most are treated as disposable.
card.light: Bright indirect light in a genuinely cool room — 12–15 °C. A cyclamen in a warm lounge collapses within a fortnight, which is why most are treated as disposable.
card.water: Water from below, into the saucer, and never into the crown. Let it take up what it wants for twenty minutes, then pour the rest away. As a starting point, water every 6 days.
card.humidity: Above 50%.
card.temperature: Likes it cool: 50–65°F (10–18°C). A warm room is what usually finishes a cyclamen — much above 70°F (21°C) it yellows and goes dormant.
card.soil: Free-draining compost with grit, and the top of the tuber left proud of the surface — buried, it rots.
card.feeding: A weak high-potash feed every two weeks while in flower.
card.repotting: Repot the dormant tuber in late summer, keeping its shoulders above the compost.

common_problems.problem: Collapsing, floppy leaves and stems
common_problems.fix: Too warm — or water in the crown. Move it somewhere cool and water from below only.

common_problems.problem: Yellow leaves in spring
common_problems.fix: Normal. It is going dormant. Stop watering, let it die back, and keep the tuber dry until late summer.

common_problems.problem: Grey fuzzy mould on the stems
common_problems.fix: Botrytis from damp still air. Remove affected parts, improve airflow, and keep water off the crown.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs — the tuber especially, which can cause heart problems in quantity.

card.summary: Bush lily: strap leaves in a flat fan and, after a cold dry winter rest, a head of orange trumpet flowers on a thick stalk. It is long-lived — plants outlive their owners — flowers best jammed in a pot it has outgrown, and is one of the few flowering plants that does well away from direct sun.
card.light: Bright indirect light, and no direct sun. Clivias flower reliably in a spot most flowering plants would sulk in.
card.water: Water when the top half is dry in the growing season. From late autumn, keep it almost completely dry and cool for eight to ten weeks — that rest is what makes it flower. As a starting point, water every 10 days.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–75°F (15–24°C). A cool, dry rest around 50–55°F (10–13°C) for six to eight weeks in winter helps it flower.
card.soil: A loam-based compost with grit. Clivia roots are thick and fleshy and rot in anything that stays wet.
card.feeding: A balanced feed monthly from spring to late summer; none in winter.
card.repotting: Only every three or four years — clivias flower best when tightly potbound, to the point of cracking the pot.

common_problems.problem: Never flowers
common_problems.fix: No winter rest. Keep it cool (around 10 °C) and nearly dry from November to January, then resume watering and it will send a stalk up.

common_problems.problem: Flower stalk stays short, flowers open inside the leaves
common_problems.fix: Too warm during the rest, or watered too early. Keep the rest cooler and wait until the stalk is clear of the leaves before watering.

common_problems.problem: Pale scorched patches
common_problems.fix: Direct sun. Move it into bright shade.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs; causes vomiting, and the bulb in quantity affects the heart.

card.summary: Amaryllis: a bulb the size of a fist that produces a thick stalk and three or four huge trumpet flowers, usually forced for Christmas. The bulb is perennial and improves with age — the trick is to let the leaves grow all summer to feed it, then give it eight to ten weeks completely dry in autumn.
card.light: Bright indirect light, and no direct sun. Clivias flower reliably in a spot most flowering plants would sulk in.
card.water: Water sparingly until the flower stalk is well up, then generously while it flowers and while the leaves grow. Stop entirely in late summer for a dry rest of eight to ten weeks, then start again. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–75°F (18–24°C) while growing; a cooler room makes the flowers last longer. Keep it above 50°F (10°C).
card.soil: A loam-based compost with grit. Clivia roots are thick and fleshy and rot in anything that stays wet.
card.feeding: A balanced feed monthly from spring to late summer; none in winter.
card.repotting: Every three or four years, with the top third of the bulb above the compost.

common_problems.problem: Leaves but no flowers
common_problems.fix: It did not get a dry rest, or the leaves were cut off too early. Let the leaves grow all summer to feed the bulb, then withhold water for eight to ten weeks in autumn.

common_problems.problem: Soft, mushy bulb
common_problems.fix: Rot from water sitting around the neck. Water around the edge of the pot and keep the top of the bulb exposed.

common_problems.problem: Red streaks on the bulb and leaves
common_problems.fix: Red blotch, a fungal disease. Remove affected tissue, keep the bulb dry, and treat with a fungicide.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs; causes vomiting, and the bulb in quantity affects the heart.

card.summary: The poinsettia: the red, pink or cream 'flowers' are bracts — coloured leaves around tiny true flowers. It is sold by the million each December and usually thrown out in January, but it can be kept as a houseplant.
card.light: Bright light, with some direct sun in winter. Keep it away from cold windows and draughts while it is in colour.
card.water: Water when the top of the compost is dry to the touch, thoroughly, and empty the saucer. It wilts and drops leaves if left dry, and rots if it stands in water. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine, away from heaters.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C). Cold, wet soil is what rots it.
card.soil: Ordinary peat-free compost with some perlite. It is a shrub, not a succulent, whatever its genus.
card.feeding: A balanced feed monthly from spring to autumn; none while it is in colour.
card.repotting: In spring, after cutting it back by about half. To colour again it needs about fourteen hours of complete darkness every night for eight weeks from early autumn.

common_problems.problem: Leaves dropping soon after you bring it home
common_problems.fix: Cold — on the way home or from a draughty window — or a sudden change. Keep it warm, above 15 °C, out of draughts and away from cold glass.

common_problems.problem: Yellowing leaves and wilting in a wet pot
common_problems.fix: Overwatering, often in a foil sleeve that holds the water. Take it out of the sleeve, or make holes in it, and let it drain.

common_problems.problem: The bracts don't colour again the next year
common_problems.fix: Its colour is triggered by long nights. From early autumn give it about fourteen hours of total darkness every night for eight weeks — even a streetlight can stop it.

card.toxicity: Mildly toxic to cats and dogs: the milky sap irritates the mouth and stomach and can cause drooling or vomiting. Its danger is often overstated, but keep it out of reach.

card.summary: The calla or arum lily: glossy, arrow-shaped leaves and elegant white, funnel-shaped spathes; the coloured callas sold as pot plants are hybrids of related species. It is not a true lily and does not carry the kidney danger true lilies pose to cats — but it is toxic, like the other arums.
card.light: Bright light, with some direct sun in the morning. In too little light the stems flop and it stops flowering.
card.water: Keep the compost damp while it is in leaf — it is thirsty. When the leaves start to yellow after flowering, cut the watering right back and let it rest. As a starting point, water every 5 days.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–75°F (15–24°C) while growing; rest the rhizome cool and dry at about 50–60°F (10–15°C).
card.soil: A rich, peat-free compost that holds moisture. The white arum lily grows in marshes in the wild; the coloured hybrids want slightly better drainage.
card.feeding: A balanced liquid feed every two weeks while it is in leaf and flower.
card.repotting: After it dies back. Calla lilies grow from rhizomes that rest for two or three months a year: let the leaves yellow, keep the pot dry and cool, then repot in fresh compost and start watering again.

common_problems.problem: Leaves yellowing after flowering
common_problems.fix: The start of its yearly rest. Water less, let the leaves die back, and keep the rhizome dry for a couple of months.

common_problems.problem: No flowers
common_problems.fix: Too little light, or no rest. Give it a bright spot and a proper dry rest each year.

common_problems.problem: Soft, rotting stems at the base
common_problems.fix: Wet while dormant, or cold and wet together. Keep it dry while it rests, and make sure the pot drains.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and people if chewed — the sap carries insoluble calcium oxalate crystals, which burn the mouth and throat. Keep it off the floor if anything in the house tastes its way through life.

card.summary: Scarlet star: a rosette of soft green straps around a vivid red, orange or yellow bract that lasts for months. The colour is bracts, not flowers.
card.light: Bright indirect light. Bromeliads take more shade than most flowering plants but need brightness to keep their colour.
card.water: Fill the central cup with water and keep it topped up, flushing it out every couple of weeks so it does not stagnate. Water the compost only lightly — the cup is the plant's real reservoir. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Above 60%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 60°F (15°C).
card.soil: Bromeliads are epiphytes with token root systems used mostly for anchorage. Orchid bark with a little compost, in a small pot, is right.
card.feeding: A very weak feed occasionally, into the central cup rather than the compost.
card.repotting: Rarely. The parent rosette flowers once and then slowly dies over a year or two, leaving pups around its base — those are what you pot on.

common_problems.problem: The parent rosette dying after flowering
common_problems.fix: Normal. Bromeliads are monocarpic: flower once, then finish. Keep the pups growing; they will flower in two or three years.

common_problems.problem: Brown crispy leaf tips
common_problems.fix: Dry air, or minerals in the cup. Raise humidity and flush the cup with rainwater regularly.

common_problems.problem: Rot at the base
common_problems.fix: The compost was kept too wet. Water the cup, not the pot.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs.

card.summary: The urn plant: stiff grey leaves banded in silvery scale, forming a watertight vase, with a spiky pink bract and small blue flowers. The vase is the plant's water supply and must be kept topped up and flushed out — the compost barely matters.

card.summary: The earth star: small, flat, star-shaped rosettes of wavy, striped leaves in pink, green and cream. Unlike most bromeliads it grows on the ground, so it roots into its compost and has no cup to fill — a good terrarium plant.
card.light: Bright indirect light. Bromeliads take more shade than most flowering plants but need brightness to keep their colour.
card.water: Water the compost when the top few centimetres are dry. It has no central cup to fill. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Above 60%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 60°F (15°C).
card.soil: A light compost with bark and perlite. Unlike most bromeliads it grows on the ground rather than on trees, and roots into the mix.
card.feeding: A very weak feed occasionally, into the central cup rather than the compost.
card.repotting: Rarely. The parent rosette flowers once and then slowly dies over a year or two, leaving pups around its base — those are what you pot on.

common_problems.problem: Brown, crisp leaf edges
common_problems.fix: Dry air. Raise the humidity; it does well in a terrarium.

common_problems.problem: Rot at the base
common_problems.fix: The compost was kept too wet. Let the top dry between waterings and make sure the pot drains.

common_problems.problem: The parent rosette fading after flowering
common_problems.fix: Normal: bromeliads flower once, then finish. Pot up the pups that form around it once they are a third of its size.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs.

card.summary: The pineapple: a rosette of stiff, spiny-edged leaves that, after two or three years and plenty of sun, sends up a single small pineapple. Many are grown from the top of a shop-bought fruit.
card.light: Bright indirect light. Bromeliads take more shade than most flowering plants but need brightness to keep their colour.
card.water: Water the compost when the top few centimetres are dry. It stores water in its leaves and tolerates drying out. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C); keep it above 60°F (15°C).
card.soil: Bromeliads are epiphytes with token root systems used mostly for anchorage. Orchid bark with a little compost, in a small pot, is right.
card.feeding: A very weak feed occasionally, into the central cup rather than the compost.
card.repotting: Rarely. The parent rosette flowers once and then slowly dies over a year or two, leaving pups around its base — those are what you pot on.

common_problems.problem: Leaves browning from the tips
common_problems.fix: Too little light, or dry, stuffy air. Move it into full sun; it is a field crop, not a forest plant.

common_problems.problem: Rot at the base
common_problems.fix: The compost stayed wet. Let it dry between waterings and use a gritty mix.

common_problems.problem: No fruit
common_problems.fix: It takes two or three years, and plenty of light. Patience, and the sunniest spot you have. Each plant fruits once and then makes pups.

card.toxicity: Not on the ASPCA's list of toxic or non-toxic plants, so we don't call it pet-safe: not being listed is not the same as being tested. Keep it out of reach of a pet that chews.

card.summary: A small air plant that grows on nothing at all — no soil, no pot — taking water and nutrients through scales on its leaves. It blushes red and puts out violet flowers when it is about to bloom, then pups from the base.
card.light: Bright indirect light. Bromeliads take more shade than most flowering plants but need brightness to keep their colour.
card.water: Soak the whole plant in a bowl of water for twenty to thirty minutes once a week, then shake it hard and lay it upside down to dry. Water trapped in the base for more than a few hours is what rots them — misting alone is not enough. As a starting point, water every 5 days.
card.humidity: Above 60%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–85°F (15–29°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C).
card.soil: No growing medium whatsoever. Sit them in a bowl, wire them to bark, or wedge them into a shell — anything that lets air get right round them.
card.feeding: A very weak bromeliad feed in the soaking water once a month.
card.repotting: Nothing to repot. Just make sure whatever it sits on lets it dry out within a few hours of watering.

common_problems.problem: Brown mushy centre, leaves pulling out
common_problems.fix: Water sat in the base after soaking. Shake hard and dry upside down after every soak. A rotted centre is fatal.

common_problems.problem: Leaves curling tighter and going brown at the tips
common_problems.fix: Thirsty. Soak weekly, more often in a dry warm room.

common_problems.problem: No colour or flowers
common_problems.fix: Not enough light. Move it brighter, out of direct sun.

card.toxicity: Not on the ASPCA's list of toxic or non-toxic plants, so we don't call it pet-safe: not being listed is not the same as being tested. Keep it out of reach of a pet that chews.

card.summary: The king of air plants: a big silver rosette of broad leaves curling into loose spirals, slow-growing and sculptural. It comes from drier country than most tillandsias, so it needs less frequent soaking and even more careful drying — water held in that tight centre rots it.
