card.summary: The pink quill: a grassy rosette with a flat, paddle-shaped pink bract from which small violet flowers emerge one or two at a time over several weeks. Unlike the air plants, it is sold and grown in a pot of bark.
card.light: Bright indirect light. Bromeliads take more shade than most flowering plants but need brightness to keep their colour.
card.water: Water the bark lightly when it is nearly dry, and mist the leaves now and then. Don't leave water standing in the base of the rosette. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Above 60%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–85°F (15–29°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C).
card.soil: A coarse, fast-draining orchid bark mix in a small pot. It uses its roots for anchoring more than for feeding, and rots in heavy compost.
card.feeding: A very weak bromeliad feed in the soaking water once a month.
card.repotting: Rarely. After flowering the parent slowly fades; pot up the pups once they are a third of its size.

common_problems.problem: The parent fading after flowering
common_problems.fix: Normal: it flowers once, then finishes. Keep the pups growing; they are the next plants.

common_problems.problem: Brown, crisp leaf tips
common_problems.fix: Dry air. Mist it, or raise the humidity.

common_problems.problem: Rot at the base
common_problems.fix: The bark stayed wet. Water less often, and use a coarser mix.

card.toxicity: Not on the ASPCA's list of toxic or non-toxic plants, so we don't call it pet-safe: not being listed is not the same as being tested. Keep it out of reach of a pet that chews.

card.summary: Basil: the supermarket pot that dies in a fortnight, almost always because it is thirty seedlings crammed into one small pot competing for light and root room. Split it into three or four pots the day you get it home, give it the sunniest windowsill you have, and take cuttings through the summer.
card.light: As much direct sun as possible. Supermarket basil dies indoors mainly because a kitchen windowsill gives it a fraction of the light it needs.
card.water: Keep the compost damp — basil wilts fast and hard — but water in the morning, at the base, so the leaves are dry by night. As a starting point, water every 3 days.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine, with air moving.
card.temperature: Wants warmth: 65–85°F (18–29°C). Below about 50°F (10°C) the leaves blacken, so never leave it on a cold windowsill overnight.
card.soil: A rich compost that holds some water but drains freely. The pot a supermarket basil comes in is far too small and far too crowded — split it into three or four pots on day one.
card.feeding: A balanced feed at half strength every two weeks in summer.
card.repotting: Basil is an annual. Rather than repotting, take cuttings through the summer and start new plants.

common_problems.problem: Whole plant collapses within a fortnight of coming home
common_problems.fix: Too many seedlings in one small pot, all competing. Split the clump into three or four pots on the day you buy it, and put it in the sunniest spot you have.

common_problems.problem: Black spots and stems going soft
common_problems.fix: Fungal disease from cold, damp, still air. Water in the morning at the base, improve airflow, and keep it warm.

common_problems.problem: Flower spikes forming
common_problems.fix: It is bolting; the leaves turn bitter afterwards. Pinch out the flower buds and the top pair of leaves regularly to keep it producing.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs, and edible.

card.summary: Spearmint: vigorous, invasive, and best kept in a pot for exactly that reason — in open ground it takes over. Indoors it wants bright light and constantly damp compost, and it should be cut back to a stub each time it goes woody, which it will.
card.light: As much direct sun as possible. Supermarket basil dies indoors mainly because a kitchen windowsill gives it a fraction of the light it needs.
card.water: Keep it damp. Mint is a streamside plant and the one herb that genuinely does not want to dry out. As a starting point, water every 3 days.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine, with air moving.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 55–75°F (13–24°C) and tolerant of cool; mint is hardy outdoors, so a chilly windowsill is no threat.
card.soil: A rich compost that holds some water but drains freely. The pot a supermarket basil comes in is far too small and far too crowded — split it into three or four pots on day one.
card.feeding: A balanced feed at half strength every two weeks in summer.
card.repotting: Every spring — mint fills a pot with runners within a season and exhausts it.

common_problems.problem: Lower stems going bare and woody
common_problems.fix: Normal after a season. Cut the whole plant back to 5 cm; it reshoots within a fortnight.

common_problems.problem: Orange spots under the leaves
common_problems.fix: Mint rust. Cut it right back, bin the affected material, and do not compost it.

card.toxicity: Mildly toxic to cats and dogs, mostly when eaten in quantity. Edible for people.

card.summary: Rosemary: a Mediterranean shrub growing on thin stony hillsides, which tells you everything about what it wants — full sun, gritty compost, and to be left dry. Indoor rosemary usually dies suddenly and without warning, and the cause is almost always a pot that stayed wet.
card.light: As much direct sun as possible. Supermarket basil dies indoors mainly because a kitchen windowsill gives it a fraction of the light it needs.
card.water: Let the pot dry out well between waterings. Indoor rosemary is almost always killed by overwatering, and it gives no warning before it goes. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine, with air moving.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 55–75°F (13–24°C). In winter it wants bright and cool, around 45–60°F (7–15°C); a warm, dry room is what kills indoor rosemary.
card.soil: Rosemary is a Mediterranean shrub growing on thin stony ground. Gritty free-draining compost, and a terracotta pot, are much closer to right than rich compost.
card.feeding: Very little — a weak feed twice over the summer.
card.repotting: Basil is an annual. Rather than repotting, take cuttings through the summer and start new plants.

common_problems.problem: Suddenly brown and dead with no warning
common_problems.fix: Root rot from a pot that stayed wet, or dried out completely once. Let the top half dry between waterings and use gritty compost in terracotta.

common_problems.problem: Powdery white mildew
common_problems.fix: Still humid air indoors. Improve airflow; rosemary is happier outdoors whenever the weather allows.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs; edible.

card.summary: Common thyme: a small, woody herb with tiny, fragrant grey-green leaves. On a windowsill it needs full sun and dry roots — like rosemary, it is far more often killed by watering than by neglect.
card.light: As much direct sun as possible. Supermarket basil dies indoors mainly because a kitchen windowsill gives it a fraction of the light it needs.
card.water: Let the pot dry out well between waterings. Indoor rosemary is almost always killed by overwatering, and it gives no warning before it goes. As a starting point, water every 6 days.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine, with air moving.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 55–75°F (13–24°C); a cool, sunny windowsill suits it.
card.soil: Rosemary is a Mediterranean shrub growing on thin stony ground. Gritty free-draining compost, and a terracotta pot, are much closer to right than rich compost.
card.feeding: Very little — a weak feed twice over the summer.

common_problems.problem: Powdery white mildew
common_problems.fix: Still humid air indoors. Improve airflow; rosemary is happier outdoors whenever the weather allows.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs; edible.

card.summary: Parsley, curly or flat-leaved: a biennial herb usually grown for a season and replaced. Supermarket pots are crowded with seedlings; split the clump into a few smaller pots and it lasts far longer.

card.water: Keep the compost damp. Parsley has a long taproot and sulks if it dries out. As a starting point, water every 3 days.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine, with air moving.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 55–75°F (13–24°C); it tolerates a cool windowsill.
card.soil: A rich compost that holds some water but drains freely. The pot a supermarket basil comes in is far too small and far too crowded — split it into three or four pots on day one.

card.summary: Chives: clumps of thin, hollow, onion-flavoured leaves, with round purple flowers in summer. One of the easiest herbs on a sunny windowsill — and, like all onions, toxic to cats and dogs.
card.light: As much direct sun as possible. Supermarket basil dies indoors mainly because a kitchen windowsill gives it a fraction of the light it needs.
card.water: Keep the compost evenly damp. As a starting point, water every 4 days.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine, with air moving.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 55–75°F (13–24°C); hardy outdoors, and happy on a cool windowsill.
card.soil: A rich compost that holds some water but drains freely. The pot a supermarket basil comes in is far too small and far too crowded — split it into three or four pots on day one.
card.feeding: A balanced feed at half strength every two weeks in summer.
card.repotting: Divide and repot every spring, and cut a tired pot back to a few centimetres to make it regrow.

common_problems.problem: Whole plant collapses within a fortnight of coming home
common_problems.fix: Too many seedlings in one small pot, all competing. Split the clump into three or four pots on the day you buy it, and put it in the sunniest spot you have.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs. Like onions and garlic, chives damage red blood cells, and cats are especially sensitive — keep them well out of reach. Edible for people.

card.summary: The Meyer lemon: a compact citrus that flowers and fruits readily in a pot, scenting a room when it blooms. It needs the brightest position you have, a citrus-specific feed, and rainwater — the yellow-with-green-veins leaves on most indoor lemons are hard water locking out iron.
card.light: As much direct sun as possible, and outdoors from late spring to autumn if you can manage it. Citrus indoors in poor light drop their leaves and never fruit.
card.water: Water thoroughly when the top few centimetres are dry, with rainwater if your tap is hard. Never let it stand in a saucer. As a starting point, water every 6 days.
card.humidity: Above 50%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–80°F (15–27°C), and fine with a cool, bright winter; keep it above 45°F (7°C).
card.soil: A free-draining, slightly acid mix. Citrus-specific composts exist and are worth using; ordinary compost plus hard water causes the yellowing you see on half the lemon trees in garden centres.
card.feeding: A citrus feed — summer formula in the growing season, winter formula from autumn. They are hungry and specific about it.
card.repotting: Every second or third spring, one size up. Prune lightly in late winter to keep the shape.

common_problems.problem: Yellow leaves with green veins
common_problems.fix: Iron or magnesium locked out by hard water or alkaline compost. Use rainwater, repot into citrus compost, and use a proper citrus feed.

common_problems.problem: Leaves dropping in winter
common_problems.fix: Too warm and too dark indoors. Keep it cool (around 10 °C) and as bright as possible over winter, and water much less.

common_problems.problem: Sticky leaves and sooty black mould
common_problems.fix: Scale insects — extremely common on indoor citrus. Check stems and leaf undersides, wipe them off, and treat every week for a month.

common_problems.problem: Flowers but no fruit
common_problems.fix: Nothing pollinated them indoors. Dab each flower with a soft brush every day or two while they are open.

card.toxicity: Mildly toxic to cats and dogs — the essential oils in the leaves and peel cause vomiting and, in cats, can irritate skin.

card.summary: The coffee plant: glossy, deeply veined dark leaves on an upright shrub, growing as understorey in the Ethiopian highlands. It makes a handsome foliage plant indoors and will, at four or five years old and in good conditions, flower and set a few cherries — enough for a novelty, not a cup.
card.light: Bright indirect light, no direct sun. Coffee grows as an understorey shrub and the leaves scorch quickly in a sunny window.
card.water: Keep evenly damp through spring and summer, slightly drier in winter. It wilts hard when dry and the leaf edges brown afterwards. As a starting point, water every 6 days.
card.humidity: Above 60%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 60°F (15°C) and away from cold windows.
card.soil: A slightly acid, free-draining mix — ericaceous compost cut with perlite works well.
card.feeding: A balanced feed at half strength every two weeks in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every spring while young. It grows into a substantial shrub and can be pruned to keep it in bounds.

common_problems.problem: Brown leaf edges and tips
common_problems.fix: Dry air or hard water. Raise the humidity above 60% and water with rainwater.

common_problems.problem: Leaves yellowing between the veins
common_problems.fix: The compost has gone too alkaline. Repot into an ericaceous mix and feed.

common_problems.problem: Leaf drop after a cold night
common_problems.fix: Cold damage — it will not take below about 12 °C. Move it away from cold glass and keep it warm.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs — the caffeine in the leaves and beans causes vomiting, a racing heart and tremors.

card.summary: The avocado, as most people grow it: from a stone, sprouted in a glass of water. It makes a fast, leafy tree indoors but almost never fruits there.
card.light: Bright light and as much direct sun as you can give it. An avocado grown from a stone stretches into a tall, bare single stem in anything less.
card.water: Water thoroughly when the top few centimetres are dry, and empty the saucer. As a starting point, water every 6 days.
card.humidity: Above 50%; the leaf tips brown in dry air.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C).
card.soil: A loam-based compost with grit or perlite. Avocados want moisture but are very prone to root rot in a wet, airless mix.
card.feeding: A balanced feed monthly in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every spring while it is young, one size up.

common_problems.problem: Brown, crispy leaf tips
common_problems.fix: Salts from tap water and fertiliser, or dry air. Flush the pot through with rainwater every few months and raise the humidity.

common_problems.problem: One tall stem with few leaves
common_problems.fix: Too little light, and no pruning. Pinch out the top when it reaches about 30 cm, and again later; it branches from below the cut.

common_problems.problem: Leaves drooping in a wet pot
common_problems.fix: Root rot. Let it dry out further and make sure the pot drains; avocados drown easily.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs, and more seriously to pet birds: the leaves, stone and skin contain persin, which causes vomiting and diarrhoea. Keep birds well away from it.

card.summary: Gold dust dracaena: slender wiry stems with oval leaves spotted in cream, looking more like a shrub than the strap-leaved dracaenas. It is slow, takes low light well, and is one of the more unusual-looking easy plants.
card.light: Medium to bright indirect light. The snake plants in this genus tolerate deep shade and full sun alike, but the leafy dracaenas — marginata, fragrans, the rest — scorch in direct sun and stretch in the dark.
card.water: Let the top half of the pot dry out for the leafy kinds; let the whole pot dry for the snake plants. Both are far more often overwatered than under. As a starting point, water every 9 days.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C) and away from cold windows.
card.soil: Free-draining is the whole requirement. Ordinary compost cut with a third perlite for the leafy kinds; cactus compost for the snake plants, which rot at the base if the mix holds water.
card.feeding: A weak balanced feed monthly in spring and summer; none in winter.
card.repotting: Every two or three years. Snake plants flower and grow best slightly potbound, so leave them until the pot is visibly straining.

common_problems.problem: Brown tips on long thin leaves
common_problems.fix: Fluoride and salts in tap water — dracaenas are unusually sensitive. Water with rainwater or filtered water, and flush the pot through a few times a year.

common_problems.problem: Soft yellow base on a snake plant, leaves falling out of the pot
common_problems.fix: Rot. Water has sat in the crown or the mix. Take the firm leaves as cuttings and start again. Water snake plants from below or around the edge, never into the centre.

common_problems.problem: Lower leaves yellowing and dropping on a cane dracaena
common_problems.fix: Normal ageing if it is one at a time; overwatering if it is several. Peel the old leaves off cleanly and check the mix is drying out between waterings.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs. The saponins cause vomiting, drooling and — in cats specifically — dilated pupils. Not dangerous to people beyond an upset stomach.

card.summary: Croton: leathery leaves splashed in yellow, orange, red and green, in leaf shapes ranging from oak to corkscrew. The colour is made by light, so a croton in a dim spot slowly turns green and stops being worth having.
card.light: Bright light with some direct sun. The colour in a croton is made by light — in a dim spot the new leaves come out plain green and the plant stops being the thing you bought.
card.water: Keep evenly damp. A croton that dries out drops every leaf, often overnight, and takes months to recover. As a starting point, water every 6 days.
card.humidity: Above 60%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C); keep it above 60°F (15°C). Cold drafts make a croton drop its leaves.
card.soil: A rich compost with perlite. Crotons want moisture and food but not a waterlogged pot.
card.feeding: A balanced feed at half strength every two weeks in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every second spring. Prune in spring if it goes bare below; it branches from the cut.

common_problems.problem: All the leaves drop at once
common_problems.fix: A shock: a move, a draught, a cold delivery van, or drying out. Keep it warm, bright, damp and still. New growth usually comes in a few weeks.

common_problems.problem: New leaves plain green
common_problems.fix: Not enough light. Move it into the brightest spot you have.

common_problems.problem: Spider mites
common_problems.fix: Dry air. Crotons attract them badly. Raise the humidity, shower it, and treat weekly for a month.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs — the milky sap irritates the mouth and causes vomiting, and it can irritate skin on contact.

card.summary: The ti plant: strap leaves in pink, red, cream and green on slim canes, grown across Polynesia for centuries for food, thatch and ceremony. Indoors it wants bright light to hold its colour and rainwater to keep its tips green — it is markedly fluoride-sensitive.
card.light: Bright light with some direct sun. The colour in a croton is made by light — in a dim spot the new leaves come out plain green and the plant stops being the thing you bought.
card.water: Keep lightly damp with rainwater. Cordylines are noticeably sensitive to fluoride in tap water and brown at the tips because of it. As a starting point, water every 6 days.
card.humidity: Above 60%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C).
card.soil: A rich compost with perlite. Crotons want moisture and food but not a waterlogged pot.
card.feeding: A balanced feed at half strength every two weeks in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every second spring. Prune in spring if it goes bare below; it branches from the cut.

common_problems.problem: Brown tips and edges
common_problems.fix: Fluoride and salts in tap water — the classic cordyline complaint. Switch to rainwater or filtered water and flush the pot occasionally.

common_problems.problem: Colour fading
common_problems.fix: Not enough light. Move it brighter.

common_problems.problem: Lower leaves yellowing and dropping
common_problems.fix: Normal as the cane lengthens. Peel them off; cut the cane back in spring if it is too bare.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs; the saponins cause vomiting, and in cats dilated pupils.

card.summary: The nerve plant: small oval leaves netted in white, pink or red veins, on a low creeping plant. It is famous for fainting — it collapses completely when the compost dries and stands back up within an hour of water.
card.light: Medium indirect light, no direct sun. Nerve plants live on a dark forest floor and scorch in a bright window.
card.water: Keep damp at all times. A fittonia faints theatrically when dry and usually recovers within an hour of water — but each faint costs it leaves. As a starting point, water every 4 days.
card.humidity: Above 70%. This is a terrarium plant that is sold as a houseplant.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 60°F (15°C) and out of drafts.
card.soil: A mix that stays damp: peat-free compost with perlite, in a small shallow pot.
card.feeding: A weak balanced feed monthly in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every spring, into a shallow pot. Pinch the tips out to keep it dense.

common_problems.problem: Dramatic total collapse
common_problems.fix: It dried out. It does this often. Water it and it stands back up within the hour. A terrarium or cloche prevents the cycle.

common_problems.problem: Crispy brown leaf edges
common_problems.fix: Air too dry. Above 70% humidity, or grow it under glass.

common_problems.problem: Leggy bare stems
common_problems.fix: Too little light, or no pinching. Pinch the tips out regularly and move it to medium indirect light.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs.

card.summary: The polka dot plant: leaves freckled in pink, white or red over green, in a small bushy plant. It is short-lived and wants pinching constantly to stay dense — once it flowers it goes leggy and tired, so pinch out the flower spikes and take cuttings each year.
card.light: Medium indirect light, no direct sun. Nerve plants live on a dark forest floor and scorch in a bright window.
card.water: Keep damp at all times. A fittonia faints theatrically when dry and usually recovers within an hour of water — but each faint costs it leaves. As a starting point, water every 4 days.
card.humidity: Above 50%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–80°F (18–27°C); keep it above 60°F (15°C).
card.soil: A mix that stays damp: peat-free compost with perlite, in a small shallow pot.
card.feeding: A weak balanced feed monthly in spring and summer.
card.repotting: It is short-lived and best replaced or restarted from cuttings every year or two. Pinch out flower spikes — flowering exhausts it.

common_problems.problem: Dramatic total collapse
common_problems.fix: It dried out. It does this often. Water it and it stands back up within the hour. A terrarium or cloche prevents the cycle.

common_problems.problem: Crispy brown leaf edges
common_problems.fix: Air too dry. Above 70% humidity, or grow it under glass.

common_problems.problem: Leggy bare stems
common_problems.fix: Too little light, or no pinching. Pinch the tips out regularly and move it to medium indirect light.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs.

card.summary: Coleus: soft, toothed leaves in almost any combination of lime, red, burgundy, pink and near-black. A fast, short-lived plant grown entirely for its colour — pinch it often, take cuttings in late summer, and start again.
card.light: Bright light with an hour or two of sun. The colours fade to a muddy green in shade, and scorch in hot midday sun.
card.water: Keep evenly damp. Coleus wilts dramatically when dry and recovers, but each wilt costs it lower leaves. As a starting point, water every 4 days.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 65–85°F (18–29°C); keep it above 55°F (13°C). Cold makes it drop leaves.
card.soil: Ordinary potting compost with some perlite. It is a fast, forgiving plant.
card.feeding: A balanced feed at half strength monthly in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Best treated as short-lived: take cuttings in late summer and start again. Pinch out the flower spikes, which end its season.

common_problems.problem: Colours fading to green
common_problems.fix: Not enough light. Move it brighter; new leaves will colour up, old ones won't.

common_problems.problem: Long bare stems
common_problems.fix: Not enough light, and no pinching. Pinch the tips regularly to make it branch, and move it brighter.

common_problems.problem: Wilting and dropping leaves
common_problems.fix: It dried out — or it sits wet. Check the compost: water if it is dry, let it drain if it is soggy.

common_problems.problem: White cottony blobs in the leaf joints
common_problems.fix: Mealybugs. Dab them with alcohol on a cotton bud every few days for a month.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs — the essential oils cause vomiting and diarrhoea, and can irritate skin.

card.summary: Purple shamrock: triangular deep-purple leaflets on thin stalks that fold down at night and open again in the morning, with small pale pink flowers. It grows from little scaly rhizomes and dies back completely once a year — which looks like death and isn't.
card.light: Bright indirect light with a little direct sun. The purple deepens in brighter light; in shade the leaves stretch and pale.
card.water: Keep lightly damp while in leaf. When it dies back, stop watering entirely until new shoots appear. As a starting point, water every 6 days.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–75°F (15–24°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C). Long spells of heat or cold can send it dormant.
card.soil: Ordinary compost with perlite. It grows from small scaly rhizomes just under the surface.
card.feeding: A balanced feed at half strength monthly while in leaf.
card.repotting: Every second spring, or whenever the pot fills with rhizomes. Divide at the same time.

common_problems.problem: Dies back to nothing in late summer
common_problems.fix: Dormancy, and completely normal. Stop watering, leave the pot somewhere cool for a month or two, then start again — it comes back thicker.

common_problems.problem: Leaves folding down
common_problems.fix: Normal. It folds at night and in strong sun. Nothing to fix.

common_problems.problem: Pale stretched stems
common_problems.fix: Not enough light. Move it brighter.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs, especially in quantity — the leaves are high in oxalic acid.

card.summary: The cast iron plant: broad dark leaves straight out of the compost, and the toughest genuinely low-light plant there is. It survived Victorian parlours lit by gas and heated by coal, which is where the name came from — and it is still the right answer for a dark hallway.
card.light: Low to medium indirect light — it is called the cast iron plant for a reason, and it is the best genuine low-light plant on this list. Direct sun scorches it.
card.water: Water when the top half of the pot is dry. It survives being forgotten for a month, which is the whole point of it. As a starting point, water every 12 days.
card.humidity: Indifferent.
card.temperature: One of the most forgiving: fine anywhere from 45–85°F (7–29°C).
card.soil: Ordinary compost with perlite. Nothing special required.
card.feeding: A weak feed two or three times over the summer. Over-feeding scorches the leaf tips.
card.repotting: Every four or five years. It is very slow and resents disturbance.

common_problems.problem: Brown leaf tips
common_problems.fix: Over-feeding, or hard water. Feed less and flush the pot with rainwater.

common_problems.problem: Pale bleached patches
common_problems.fix: Direct sun. Move it into shade.

common_problems.problem: Very slow growth
common_problems.fix: Normal. Two or three new leaves a year is a good year. Nothing to fix; do not over-water trying to speed it up.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs.

card.summary: Umbrella papyrus: tall thin stems topped with a whorl of narrow bracts like the spokes of an umbrella. It is a marsh plant and the one houseplant that genuinely cannot be overwatered — stand the pot permanently in a saucer of water and it will thank you.
card.light: Bright light, including some direct sun. It is a marsh plant from open ground.
card.water: Stand the pot in a saucer of water and keep it there. An umbrella plant cannot be overwatered and dies quickly if it dries. As a starting point, water every 3 days.
card.humidity: Above 50%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–80°F (15–27°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C).
card.soil: Ordinary compost, kept wet. This is the one houseplant that is genuinely happy with its pot standing in water.
card.feeding: A balanced feed monthly through the growing season.
card.repotting: Every spring — it fills a pot fast.

common_problems.problem: Brown crispy stem tips
common_problems.fix: It dried out, even briefly. Stand it in water permanently.

common_problems.problem: Yellowing older stems
common_problems.fix: Normal ageing. Cut them out at the base.

card.toxicity: Not on the ASPCA's list of toxic or non-toxic plants, so we don't call it pet-safe: not being listed is not the same as being tested. Keep it out of reach of a pet that chews.

card.summary: Baby's tears: a dense mat of tiny round leaves that spills over the edge of a pot like green foam. It needs constant damp and collapses within hours of drying out, which makes it a good terrarium groundcover and a demanding pot plant.
card.light: Medium indirect light, no direct sun. Nerve plants live on a dark forest floor and scorch in a bright window.
card.water: Keep damp at all times, watering from below. Baby's tears collapses within hours of drying out. As a starting point, water every 3 days.
card.humidity: Above 70%. This is a terrarium plant that is sold as a houseplant.
card.temperature: Prefers it cool: 55–75°F (13–24°C). Warm rooms dry it out fast; it tolerates cold down to about 45°F (7°C).
card.soil: A mix that stays damp: peat-free compost with perlite, in a small shallow pot.
card.feeding: A weak balanced feed monthly in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every spring, into a shallow pot. Pinch the tips out to keep it dense.

common_problems.problem: Dramatic total collapse
common_problems.fix: It dried out. It does this often. Water it and it stands back up within the hour. A terrarium or cloche prevents the cycle.

common_problems.problem: Crispy brown leaf edges
common_problems.fix: Air too dry. Above 70% humidity, or grow it under glass.

common_problems.problem: Leggy bare stems
common_problems.fix: Too little light, or no pinching. Pinch the tips out regularly and move it to medium indirect light.

card.toxicity: Non-toxic to cats and dogs.

card.summary: Asparagus fern: soft, flat, feathery sprays that look like fern fronds and aren't — this is a relative of edible asparagus, with true leaves reduced to scales. It is tougher than any real fern, grows from a mass of water-storing tubers, and is toxic to cats and dogs, unlike the ferns it imitates.
card.light: Medium indirect light, and never direct sun. A bright north window or a well-lit bathroom is close to ideal.
card.water: Keep the compost lightly damp in spring and summer, letting the top few centimetres dry between waterings. The tubers store water, so it forgives a missed watering far better than a real fern — but not a pot left standing wet. As a starting point, water every 5 days.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine; more keeps the foliage fuller.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–75°F (15–24°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C).
card.soil: A mix that holds water without turning to mud: compost with perlite and a little bark. Ferns have fine roots that must never dry out completely.
card.feeding: A weak balanced feed monthly in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every spring. Divide the clump at the same time if it has filled the pot.

common_problems.problem: Yellowing, shedding needles
common_problems.fix: Too dark, or the pot dried right out. Move it brighter and water more regularly. Cut bare stems back to the base; new ones come up from the tubers.

common_problems.problem: Yellowing stems in a pot that stays wet
common_problems.fix: Overwatering — the tubers rot if they sit wet. Let the top third dry out between waterings, and make sure the pot drains.

common_problems.problem: Fine webbing and pale speckling
common_problems.fix: Spider mites, which like its dense foliage in dry air. Shower it thoroughly and treat every week for a month.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs. The berries cause vomiting and the sap can give a skin rash — and despite the name it is not a fern at all, but a relative of asparagus.

card.summary: Foxtail fern and Sprenger's asparagus are two forms of this one tough, tuberous-rooted plant: Sprenger's arches and trails, while the foxtail form grows dense upright plumes. Not a fern at all, and much more drought-tolerant than one.
card.light: Medium indirect light, and never direct sun. A bright north window or a well-lit bathroom is close to ideal.
card.water: Keep the compost lightly damp in spring and summer, letting the top few centimetres dry between waterings. The tubers store water, so it forgives a missed watering far better than a real fern — but not a pot left standing wet. As a starting point, water weekly.
card.humidity: Room humidity is fine; more keeps the foliage fuller.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–75°F (15–24°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C).
card.soil: A mix that holds water without turning to mud: compost with perlite and a little bark. Ferns have fine roots that must never dry out completely.
card.feeding: A weak balanced feed monthly in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every spring. Divide the clump at the same time if it has filled the pot.

common_problems.problem: Yellowing, shedding needles
common_problems.fix: Too dark, or the pot dried right out. Move it brighter and water more regularly. Cut bare stems back to the base; new ones come up from the tubers.

common_problems.problem: Yellowing stems in a pot that stays wet
common_problems.fix: Overwatering — the tubers rot if they sit wet. Let the top third dry out between waterings, and make sure the pot drains.

common_problems.problem: Fine webbing and pale speckling
common_problems.fix: Spider mites, which like its dense foliage in dry air. Shower it thoroughly and treat every week for a month.

card.toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs. The berries cause vomiting and the sap can give a skin rash — and despite the name it is not a fern at all, but a relative of asparagus.

card.summary: Common bamboo: a true woody bamboo, fast, thirsty and demanding of light, which grows into a substantial clump in a large pot.
card.light: Bright indirect light. True bamboos want brightness and airflow; they do poorly in a dark corner.
card.water: Keep the compost damp at all times. Bamboo in a pot dries out fast and drops leaves when it does. As a starting point, water every 5 days.
card.humidity: Above 50%.
card.temperature: Comfortable at 60–85°F (15–29°C); keep it above 50°F (10°C).
card.soil: A rich compost that holds water. Bamboo is thirsty and roots hard into whatever it is given.
card.feeding: A high-nitrogen feed every two weeks in spring and summer.
card.repotting: Every spring — bamboo fills a pot with root in a single season and will eventually split it.

common_problems.problem: Leaves curling lengthways
common_problems.fix: Thirsty. Water more often; potted bamboo needs it almost daily in summer.

common_problems.problem: Yellow leaves
common_problems.fix: Overwatering in a pot with no drainage, or hard water. Check the pot drains; use rainwater.

common_problems.problem: Spider mites
common_problems.fix: Dry indoor air. Raise humidity and treat weekly.

card.toxicity: Not on the ASPCA's list of toxic or non-toxic plants, so we don't call it pet-safe: not being listed is not the same as being tested. Keep it out of reach of a pet that chews.
